#7813. The Best Compost Tumblers of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

By Jenn Ryan, Glenda Taylor, Additional research provided by Mark Wolfe

Published Oct 30, 2026 9:00 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Composting has numerous benefits, and having a compost tumbler makes the process even easier. In addition to recycling kitchen, lawn, and garden waste into a helpful soil amendment, composting helps keep significant amounts of organic waste out of landfills. As lawn care and gardening enthusiasts, we wanted to find out just how easy these contraptions made the task, so we tested several. For 8 weeks, we filled and turned tumblers, yielding over 100 pounds of plant-enriching compost.

After testing, we selected the RSI Maze 65-Gallon Compost Tumbler as our favorite due to its overall ease of use and smart design, but it’s not the only great option. Ahead, learn more about how these products fared in testing, and discover which considerations are worth bearing in mind when you’re shopping for the best compost tumbler.

Bottom line: Compost tumblers simplify composting, offering various features to suit different needs. Our tests highlight top models for efficiency and ease of use.

We tested each of these composters, from assembly to everyday use, to determine the best picks for both small and large home gardens.

The 65-gallon RSI Maze Compost Tumbler makes controlling the bin simple and smooth, even when fully loaded, with a geared handle and ratchet lock. The bin features air vents on all sides and large sliding covers that simplify loading and unloading. The dual-chamber design facilitates a consistent flow of garden waste in and compost out. This is a suitable size for medium to large gardens and landscapes.

The 65-gallon (8.69-cubic-foot) bin is made of UV-protected high-impact plastic. The frame is made of rust- and corrosion-resistant zinc-coated steel. It offers 15 inches of ground clearance for unloading compost via a cart.

We loved the size of this composter as well as its hand crank, which made it easy to turn even when the composter was full. We filled it with organic vegetable and fruit scraps, dry leaves, and dry grass.

This tumbler’s crank was a unique feature. Rather than having to roll the barrel, the crank allowed us to turn the bin with ease and “stop” it in a position where it was easiest to empty it. It is heavy, though, so users should be mindful of where to place it. Once it’s full, it’s difficult to move.

What our tester says: “I found this product to be high quality. It’s very durable, thanks in part to its rust-resistant zinc coating. Additionally, it’s relatively simple to assemble, and it’s easy to use.”—Jenn Ryan, Product Reviews tester and writer

Read our full review: RSI Maze Two-Stage Compost Tumbler

Get the RSI compost tumbler at Amazon, Lowe’s, Tractor Supply Co., or The Home Depot.

The FCMP Half-Size Rolling Composter is a compact, affordable pick ideal for one or two people who don’t generate much compostable waste. The ground-rolling design gives this unit a low profile that easily tucks away in small spaces, such as a balcony, patio, or garage. Built-in ergonomic handholds help make rolling less awkward. Aeration holes and deep fins break up clumps inside the chamber to maximize oxygen penetration.

The 19-gallon (2.5-cubic-foot) bin is made of recycled UV-inhibited BPA-free polyethylene. To speed decomposition, the manufacturer recommends turning the bin about twice a day.

The assembly of this product couldn’t have been easier. The composter came almost completely assembled—all we needed to do was place it on the stand and slide the door on. Although we loved the size and portability of this composter, it was too small for a large garden and would make a better option for urban composters, those with a small garden, or those who want to use compost for indoor or potted plants.

During testing, the composter needed to be turned frequently; for balance, using two hands was best. We also found it challenging to turn because it is not attached to the base; it merely sits on the stand, and both the stand and the composter can slide off balance. We found that the turning process was best done slowly, but people with mobility challenges may find this composter difficult to use, as it’s low to the ground and needs to be turned by hand.

We also found that the door was a bit tight and tricky to open and close when filling with compost and emptying. For emptying, the composter needs to be lifted, which can also be a challenge when it is full and heavy.

Overall, this composter makes a great option for those with smaller gardens, those who want zero-fuss assembly, or those who want a small but sturdy composter they can easily store out of sight.

Get the FCMP half-size compost tumbler at Amazon.

The Miracle-Gro Tumbling Composter provides a convenient place to recycle veggie scraps and houseplant debris while fitting easily into a small space. The hexagonal 18.5-gallon (2.47-cubic-foot) chamber features aeration holes and mixing bars for better oxygen infusion. Tight-locking slide doors keep out pests. For easy loading and unloading, toppers on the frame lock the bin rotation.

The UV-protected plastic chamber is built to withstand exposure to weather. The powder-coated stainless steel frame makes it easy not only to load, unload, and rotate the bin, but also to sweep or blow out debris from underneath. The composter requires some assembly, but that is made easy with step-by-step directions via a QR code. The package includes a pair of water-resistant, no-slip grip garden gloves.

Assembly for this composter was simple thanks to the included QR code that walked us through each step with 3D images—no app download required. We loved that this composter was easier to turn in a more compact size—perfect for one- or two-person households with small gardens or for urban gardeners. Since it is a smaller size, we found that the bin remained easy to turn even as it filled with compost. Its small size also makes it convenient for placing in a more conspicuous location as opposed to large dual-bin composters.

On the downside, we found that the door on this compost bin was a bit too tight and difficult to open with one hand. The frame of the composter is narrow, and combined with the fact that the composter is just inches from the ground means only a shallow dish or trough will fit under the frame to empty the compost. (In testing, we used an old sled for emptying and transporting the compost out of this tumbler.)

Get the Miracle-Gro compost tumbler at Amazon.

The RSI Maze 48‑gallon compost tumbler can be used for uninterrupted composting thanks to its dual-chamber design. The geared crank handle made turning easy, even when loaded. We liked its UV-protected barrel and galvanized steel frame, which are made especially for outdoor use.

Assembly posed a small challenge as some of the components were pretty tight and had to be forced into place. But once built, it worked smoothly and reliably. The sliding doors and ratchet lock held the drum in position, allowing easy collection of finished compost into a cart or bucket placed underneath.

The only drawback we noted was the assembly process, but that’s a one‑time obstacle worth dealing with as the daily ease and performance thereafter make up for it. Overall, the Maze tumbler delivers high usability with long-term value and minimal maintenance.

Get the Maze compost tumbler at The Home Depot.

We found the Genesis compost tumbler to be robust yet compact enough for backyard composting. We’re sold on its “rodent‑proof” design, too. Its secure sliding doors and solid construction succeeded in keeping the little critters out during our testing. We also liked the internal mixing rods and multiple ventilation points—the compost in this tumbler seemed to biodegrade more quickly than in the others we tested.

Despite its sturdy materials and tight assembly, we found it lightweight enough to rotate comfortably. Its design takes up only a small footprint but still offers substantial capacity. The UV-resistant barrel and powder-coated frame are built for long-term outdoor exposure.

On the downside, we think the doors could be wider, which would making loading and removing compost slightly less cumbersome. Still, for its build quality, ease of use, and continuous composting capability, we think the Genesis tumbler is a solid value.

Get the Genesis compost tumbler at Amazon, Tractor Supply Co., or The Home Depot.

This tumbler earned its keep with a design built for efficiency and ease of use. Its dual‑compartment barrel allowed us to continue adding fresh scraps while older material matures in the opposite chamber. For anyone serious about continuous composting, a dual chamber is essential.

Made of steel, the two‑leg stand not only gives the tumbler a solid foundation but also elevates it off the ground, offering added protection against rodents. We found this model especially well made and sturdy.

We only had one gripe: the doors had a tendency to slide open at times as we rotated the barrels. Once, we were turning the handle while looking at something else, and we lost about half of our compost before we noticed. We ended up taping the doors shut to keep them closed. Still, it might just have been our model, and this tumbler is otherwise well-built.

Get the Exaco compost tumbler at Amazon, Lowe’s, The Home Depot, or Walmart.

With its built-in, wheeled tea-collecting base, the Good Ideas compost tumbler does double duty. It comes with a rugged, FDA-approved recycled plastic body, and upon arrival, it was fully assembled, so we didn’t have to put anything together. That was impressive.

Its twist-off lids provide a tight closure, backing up the manufacturer’s claims that it’s pet- and rodent-safe. We liked how durable and easy to use this model was from day one. It sits low, so there’s no chance of it blowing over in high winds. The compact yet spacious barrel is a boon for busy gardeners who want to produce a good amount of compost.

However, the large capacity means that once we got it full, rotating the tumbler required significant effort, as the material inside got heavier. Despite that, we think this model is likely to last for years, and with its compost tea collection, it’s a hard one to beat.

What our tester said: “The Good Ideas compost tumbler really impressed me—not only is it pest-proof and made from high-quality materials, it also produces compost tea for fertilizing my plants.”—Glenda Taylor, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Good Ideas compost tumbler at Amazon, Tractor Supply Co., or Walmart.

We tested the best compost tumblers using a rubric that scored assembly, ease of use, and mobility when empty and full. We also noted the quality of instructions, including whether physical and digital versions were available. Each model was loaded with a mix of wet and dry compost materials—fruit and vegetable scraps, herbs, leaves, and grass—to evaluate how easy it was to turn under different conditions.

Points were awarded based on performance, with higher scores going to models that were simpler to assemble, turn, and empty. After testing, we averaged the points to determine our Best Overall pick and to rank the remaining models by their standout features.

Several characteristics can help shoppers determine which tumbler is the best composting tumbler for their needs. The type, intended use of the bin, amount of space available, and garden environment are some of the key considerations, as well as a few more, all detailed below.

Composting outdoors uses aerobic (i.e., oxygen-loving) microorganisms to break down organic waste quickly. Previously, home gardeners had to turn their compost piles manually with a garden fork to supply adequate oxygen. Compost tumblers, on the other hand, fully enclose the pile inside a vented barrel. They are mounted on a frame to make the barrel easier to turn, which eliminates the slow, back-breaking process of turning with a fork. The most important difference among the types of compost tumblers is in the way they turn. The tumblers rotate by one of three turning methods: ground rolling, central axis, and handle-operated.

A ground-rolling spinning compost bin has two separate pieces: the barrel (or bin) and the base. The base has a curved upper surface that cradles the bin, holding it in place without fasteners. Rollers built into the curved surface of the base allow the loaded bin to spin freely when pushed or pulled.

Because they sit at ground level, ground-rolling compost tumblers are a good choice for those who live in cold climates. The reduced exposure to wind and cold allows the bin to retain heat. The added warmth keeps composting microbes active instead of allowing them to go dormant in the cold.

Central-axis compost tumblers are built on a metal compost tumbler framework with an axle running through the midpoint of the bin. The framework serves two purposes. First, it elevates the bin to a height that reduces bending and stooping while filling, turning, and emptying the bin. Second, the axle allows the bin to spin freely to aerate its contents.

Central-axis compost bins are a good choice for those who suffer from back problems, since these bins allow the user to load and unload the material from a standing position rather than a stooping one. Some models also feature wheels, so users can easily relocate the bin to a different area of the yard or garden.

Handle-operated compost tumblers use gears to make turning the barrel much easier. The geared handle matches up with a gear built into the end of the bin. When the operator cranks the handle, it turns the bin in a smooth, controlled manner.

Handle-operated tumblers require less physical strength than other types of tumblers. This kind of tumbler might be a good choice for children, older adults, or gardeners with reduced physical strength. Buyers can also find a few electric composters that generate their own heat and are designed to be used indoors.

Before buying one, shoppers will want to determine exactly how they intend to use the bin. For instance, will it be used primarily for kitchen scrap disposal with a countertop composter like a Vego composter? Or, will it also process weeds, grass clippings, and other garden debris? Will it be filled irregularly, with additional content added periodically until it’s full? Or will it receive a steady stream of material on a regular basis?

For processing small amounts of kitchen scraps and occasional houseplant debris, a compost tumbler in the 15- to 25-gallon size range works well. To compost greater quantities on an irregular basis, such as at the end of a gardening season, large compost tumbler (50 to 80 gallons) can meet that challenge. For a steady stream of debris, dual composter tumblers can easily handle consistent loads, as they process and finish compost on one side while the user feeds new material on the other.

Indoor countertop models make good composting for beginners, since they do all the work for you. Using an indoor countertop model can let you see if composting is something you want to do on a larger scale.

Although some versions use steel, compost tumblers typically have an ultraviolet (UV)-protected plastic bin with a frame made of tubular steel or plastic. Since plastic resists both weather and corrosion and transfers heat slowly, it makes an ideal material for the bin.

Metal compost tumblers allow internal heat to escape more quickly in cold weather, slowing the composting process, and they can corrode over time. Tubular steel frames are the standard for central-axis and handle-operated tumblers. Most ground-rolling bins feature a plastic base, some of which include a reservoir for capturing the liquid runoff from the bin, called “compost tea,” another useful gardening medium.

Indoor models (like the Lomi Composter we tested) contain additional materials, such as silicone, that are designed to seal the unit, minimizing odor.

Bin capacity is measured in either gallons or cubic feet; 1 cubic foot equals 7.48 gallons. The smallest compost tumblers hold about 15 gallons, or about 2 cubic feet, while the largest holds more than 80 gallons, or 10.7 cubic feet.

Shoppers will also want to consider the amount of material and how often they want to compost. Typically, it takes at least 10 weeks to fully process a batch of compost. For this reason, many gardeners operate two tumblers simultaneously or use a dual-chamber tumbler. With a dual-chamber bin, users can add to one bin for 10 weeks, then close it, allow it to process, and gradually fill the second bin.

Tumbling helps provide air to compost and reduce moisture, both of which are vital in the decomposition process. Look for a compost bin with built-in aeration structures, such as air holes or vents in the walls, fins on the interior walls, flat sides, and mixing bars.

As the material inside breaks down, it can become compacted. Turning the bin loosens the material and breaks down the clumps. Air holes and vents allow the exchange of gases in the microorganisms within the decaying matter, letting excess moisture escape. Flat walls, such as in a hexagonal shape, force the material to tumble rather than slide. Additional texture comes from features such as fins and bars that help stir the material and add oxygen.

An enclosed compost tumbler also helps composters avoid pests like rodents and insects. The lids on these units thread, latch, or slide into tracks, which prevents rodents and other small animals from entering. Durable, heavy-duty plastic is difficult for rodents to chew through, and steel makes the bin virtually impossible to penetrate. Bears even find them challenging—though we don’t suggest putting that claim to the test if you don’t have to! Avoid adding animal favorites, such as meat scraps, bones, and items with high fat content, to the bin.

A foul odor emanating from the bin is an indication that the compost is either poorly aerated or that the carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of the compost ingredients is out of balance. Compost tumblers are specially designed to deal with the first issue quickly and easily. Simply rotating the bin once or twice each week infuses oxygen into the mix and promotes the growth of beneficial aerobic-composting microbes. If the compost smells like rotten eggs, it needs air. In that case, simply spin the bin.

Just as keeping a pet requires consistent care and attention, so does composting, only in this case, the “pets” are millions of aerobic microbes. These microbes need a consistently warm, moist environment with the right kind of “food.” Their food initially consists of about 30 parts carbon to 1 part nitrogen. Nitrogen comes from green compost ingredients, such as vegetable scraps, coffee grounds, and grass clippings. Carbon comes from so-called brown ingredients, such as autumn leaves, straw, sawdust, and paper. One way to ensure an adequate supply of carbon with kitchen scraps is to include paper products, like coffee filters, used paper towels, and tea bags, in the mix. When users add new scraps to the bin, they can cover the scraps with shredded newsprint or cardboard.

A properly working compost tumbler should heat up from the activity of the microbes and produce a somewhat sweet, earthy scent. If the ingredients are far out of balance, the microbes cannot process the compost efficiently, possibly causing unpleasant odors. If the mixture is slimy or has an ammonia odor, the nitrogen level is too high. It needs brown ingredients. If too much carbon is in the bin, it won’t heat properly; it needs green ingredients.

Compost tumblers offer numerous advantages over stationary compost piles. For starters, they’re neat. They enclose the mess for a tidier appearance. Moreover, they’re fast and easy to turn. Users only have to spin the tumbler for a minute or two instead of the half hour that it takes to turn a compost pile with a garden fork. Gardeners can move them into a garden shed or garage for efficient winter composting; however, a stationary pile simply goes dormant during cold weather.

Of course, different gardeners may have unique needs or physical limitations that impact how easily they can use a compost tumbler. Generally speaking, to distribute the compost, users can simply dump it from an elevated bin into a wheelbarrow. However, cold-weather gardeners who process compost outdoors may prefer a bin that sits directly on the ground. This is because a tumbler on an elevated frame would be exposed to cold on all sides; the composting process would slow down and stop with the rapid cool down. A bin directly on the ground would be insulated from that effect longer.

But some characteristics appeal to almost everyone. A wider opening makes it easier to load and unload, and, unlike latches and threaded lids, sliding covers rarely get clogged with debris. Exterior handgrips on the bin or a hand crank make it easier to rotate the bin.

There are several benefits of composting with a tumbler, with one of the largest draws being its impact on reducing landfill waste. On top of that, users get to take advantage of their own compost to promote a healthy garden, landscape, and houseplants. It also helps avoid the traditional downsides of composting: the amount of work involved, the mess and odors associated with it, the fear of attracting animal pests, and more. Compost tumblers eliminate these nuisances.

New to composting? Keep reading to learn more about using and maintaining your new compost tumbler.

Set up the outdoor compost tumbler in a sunny location to promote the rapid growth of composting microbes. Fill it (either all at once or over several weeks) with a mix of kitchen scraps, shredded newspaper, garden debris, grass clippings, fallen leaves, and other scraps. Moisten the mixture (it should feel like a not-quite-saturated sponge) and close the lid.

The time it takes to make compost varies depending on the temperature, time of year, and the balance of the ingredients inside. It’s possible to have garden-ready compost within 10 weeks if all of the right conditions come together.

For optimal processing and to eliminate odors, turn the compost tumbler two to three times per week—or more often if the manufacturer recommends it.

The compost should have the feel of a gently wrung-out sponge. As the material is processed and builds heat, moisture evaporates. Check the bin weekly and add water as needed.

Not usually—when properly sealed, compost tumblers deter pests far better than open compost piles.

Yes, air holes promote oxygen flow, prevent odors, and support the microbes responsible for decomposition.

#7812. Is That Really A Service Dog?

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

For years, business owners and property managers have wrestled with the same question: how do you tell the difference between a legitimate service animal and a pet that someone is trying to pass off as one?

Itâs a question John Bradford spent years trying to answer, first as a property manager overseeing thousands of rental units, and now as the founder of PetScreening, a platform used to verify animal accommodation requests across more than 7 million rental units nationwide.

With the rising number of service dogs and emotional support animals leading to incidents of confusion, conflict, and exploitation, John sets the record straight on how to verify a real service animal from one that isn't, and what you are legally allowed to ask.

The truth is that most people donât fully understand the laws around service animals and emotional support animals, and even well-meaning questions can come across as anything but. That gray area and confusion can create real risk. Ask the wrong question, and a business can face a discrimination complaint. Ask no questions at all, and policies and rules become easy to bend, which leads to potentially dangerous situations.

Getting this right protects everyone involved, including the people who genuinely rely on these animals every day.

Under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), service animals are defined as:

âDogs that are individually trained to do work or perform tasks for people with disabilities.â

Disabilities vary widely, from physical and sensory to psychiatric, intellectual, and neurological. The needs of each person are different, so the trained tasks may look different from person to person.  The ADA cites that the service animal must be a dog or, in rare cases, a miniature horse. Federal law does not require certifications, registrations, vests, or ID cards for these animals.

Beyond the specification that the animal must be trained to perform tasks, the legal standard is limited, so it can be difficult to easily identify which animals are legitimately service dogs and which are not. This is where public confusion starts.

There are plenty of ways to make a dog look like a service animal, like labeled vests, âregistrationâ certifications, and IDs, but none of these are federally supported. A dog wearing a vest isnât automatically a service animal, and a dog without one isnât automatically a pet. What matters legally is not appearance or paperwork. Itâs the dogâs trained ability to perform certain tasks.

This is the distinction many find hardest to grasp, and it matters because different laws apply to each. Service dogs are protected under the ADA and, due to their training and the tasks they perform, they are permitted in public spaces such as restaurants, retail stores, and hotels. That could mean guiding someone who is visually impaired, alerting an owner to an oncoming seizure, or reminding them to take medication. Service animals are also protected under the Fair Housing Act and require paperwork if the disability or need for the animal is not obviously understood.

Emotional support animals (ESAs) are different. Their value comes from the comfort their presence provides. They donât necessarily have to be dogs, they arenât required to be trained to perform specific tasks, and theyâre not covered by the ADA to be allowed in public spaces like restaurants.

They are, however, protected by the Fair Housing Act. Under this, landlords are generally required to make allowances for an ESA if a tenant has appropriate documentation from a licensed healthcare provider establishing a disability-related need. Examples of disabilities warranting an ESA include, but are not limited to, anxiety disorders or autism.

ESA accommodations are supposed to come through legitimate means, typically an established relationship with a licensed medical or mental health professional who can document the need. But some people have found loopholes for this by filling out forms online or paying fees for instant letters, which only fuels public skepticism about the legitimate need for these animals. Not to mention, this abuse can make people wary of service dogs, too.

While there is no foolproof visual test, trained service animals typically display consistent, recognizable behaviors. These dogs show exemplary discipline and obedience to the commands of their handler. They have the ability to ignore external distractions from other dogs, people, food, sounds, and smells while focusing on the needs of their handler. They display a calm temperament and are not aggressive or anxious. It is also expected that these animals be quiet, unless they are tasked with alerting an owner to a medical issue, and that they are housebroken and trained to walk on a leash without unnecessary pulling or circling.

This is where business owners and landlords need to tread carefully. When it isnât obvious that a dog is a service animal, staff are permitted to ask:

Is this dog required because of a disability?

What task has it been trained to perform?

Thatâs the full extent of it. Staff should not ask about the nature of a personâs disability, demand documentation or proof of training, or require dogs to demonstrate their tasks. Asking beyond the two questions, even if it comes from a place of genuine curiosity or caution, can expose a business to discrimination claims.

News stories about supposed service animals harming bystanders in public continue to raise questions about the legitimacy of those animals, and businesses are often caught in the crossfire. These incidents are symptoms of a larger problem: businesses and property owners navigating without clear guidance, while people with legitimate needs are met with suspicion.

Service animals and emotional support animals play an essential role in the lives of the people who rely on them, and protecting that role starts with understanding the rules.

If you own a business or manage a property, you donât need to become legal experts overnight, but you do need a consistent, fair process that respects peopleâs rights and keeps everyone safe. When everyone knows where the lines are, the people who truly depend on these animals can go about their lives without facing doubt at every door.

#7811. Ask Dr. Paola - HELP! What Happens If Cherry Eye Is Left Untreated? (November 2, 2026)

âHaveâ a âquestion? Send it in here!

My dog, Reggie, has Cherry eye. If left untreated, can it have a negative effect on his vision? Money is an issue for me right now.â

Cherry eye happens when the gland of the third eyelid, which helps produce tears, slips out of its normal position and becomes visible as a pink or red cherry-looking bulge in the corner of your dog's eye. I understand that veterinary expenses can be difficult to manage, and it is important to know what needs attention right away and what can safely wait a bit longer.

Cherry eye does not usually cause blindness directly, but leaving it untreated can put Reggie's eye health at risk. The exposed gland can become irritated, inflamed, or damaged, and its tear production may be reduced over time. Because this gland contributes to keeping the eye moist and protected, reduced tear production can increase the risk of dry eye, a condition that can lead to corneal damage, scarring, and impaired vision if it becomes severe. Think of the gland as part of the eye's built-in lubrication system. Even if the eye looks comfortable today, problems can develop gradually.

If surgery is not financially possible right now, please arrange a veterinary examination to confirm the diagnosis, assess tear production, and check the cornea.

Talk to your vet about a payment plan, or you might be able to find a veterinary teaching hospital or nonprofit clinic that may offer lower-cost care. Your veterinarian may recommend a suitable lubricating eye product while you work toward surgery, but lubrication will not reposition the gland. Please make sure you avoid human eye drops, leftover medications, or steroid eye drops unless specifically prescribed, as some of these can worsen an undiagnosed corneal ulcer. The gland should generally be repositioned and preserved rather than removed. If the gland is removed, you would need to use eye drops to supplement Reggieâs tear production for the rest of his life.

Please seek same-day veterinary care if you see Reggie squinting, holding the eye closed, rubbing it persistently, developing a cloudy or bluish cornea, or producing thick yellow or green discharge. These can be signs of a painful or more serious eye problem. If the eye is comfortable and clear, it may not be an immediate emergency, but I would not leave cherry eye unassessed for weeks or months. The most important first step is protecting the eye while finding an affordable treatment option.

Most carved pumpkins tend to get binned or left rotting on the curb once the candles burn out. Yet that leftover gourdish grin is packed with benefits for your soil, future plants, and wildlife

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The first few days of November bring a familiar sorry sight, as pumpkins start piling up beside the trash cans, a few of them still grinning. Millions end up in landfills every year, where they break down without much air and give off greenhouse gases. That's a poor end for leftover Halloween pumpkins. In a garden, all that soft tissue could be breaking down into organic matter and feeding soil life – and that’s just the start.

If you took the time to grow pumpkins for Halloween, you know how much space, moisture, and fertilizer a single vine demands. All summer long, its leaves absorbed sunlight and pumped nutrients directly into its swollen fruit. Letting those nutrients leave your yard in a trash bag deprives your yard of valuable goodness that could be benefiting vegetable beds, feeding organisms and helping beneficial creatures. Even a carved pumpkin can have a second life as long as it hasn't been painted or coated.

Giving your post-Halloween gourds a productive second act is simple, fun, and satisfying. The only rule is that your fruit needs to be clean and free of contaminants. Any sections coated in craft paints, glitter, chemical sealants, or fake snow must be removed and tossed into the trash. Pull out any burnt candle stubs, melted wax, and battery-powered tea lights, and you are ready to put this fall bounty to work!

Turning post-holiday pumpkins into garden assets is a real no-brainer. Standard carving pumpkin varieties like Howden and Jack O' Lantern work especially well for the soil, because their flesh is tender and relatively easy to slice. Thicker, denser culinary and heirloom varieties (such as ribbed Cinderella, dusty-blue Jarrahdale, or warty Marina di Chioggia) offer firmer rinds that hold their shape for weeks, making them ideal where shape and rigidity are useful.

These fall projects work across every USDA hardiness zone, though local temperatures will determine how quickly your gourd decomposes. In cold northern regions (zones 3-5), freezing nights preserve carved pumpkins on porches longer, but freeze-thaw cycles eventually cause cell walls to collapse into watery slop, making early November the best time to act. In warm southern places (zones 8-10), elevated daytime temperatures accelerate mold and fruit flies, requiring immediate conversion into ground-based or wildlife-specific benefits.

Before tackling these projects, you need the right hand tools. A heavy-duty hori-hori knife is an excellent investment if you don’t have one, and can be used to simplify all kinds of cutting work. The Nisaku Hori-Hori from Amazon is great value and makes slicing through thick rinds a joy, and levers drainage holes through thick base walls without snapping. So find out exactly why your grinning pumpkin still has lots of goodness to give…

Tossing an intact pumpkin onto your compost heap can lead to disappointment. Its waxy rind acts like a raincoat, and depending on the variety and the weather, it could sit there for a long time with its skin intact. It needs breaking up first. Take a sharp spade or round-point shovel, and break the fruit down into fist-sized chunks to expose the flesh to soil bacteria and fungi.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Because the tissue is roughly 90% water, this green compost source needs plenty of dry browns mixed in. Balance every bucket of chopped pumpkin with two buckets of carbon-rich browns, such as shredded leaves, straw, or torn cardboard to keep the pile aerated. Turn the heap now and then. If space is tight, a single-chamber tumbler like the Vivosun Outdoor Dual Chamber Tumbling Composter, available from Amazon speeds up heat decomposition in a more compact way.

If your compost heap is overflowing, try direct trench composting in an empty veg bed. Dig a trench 18-24 inches (45-61cm) deep, in a bed reserved for heavy-feeding spring crops like sweet corn, squash, or tomatoes. Fill the bottom with chopped chunks and stomp them down. Backfill with 12 inches (30cm) of clean soil. Don’t go shallower, or neighborhood raccoons may smell it and dig it back up. Loose, well-drained soil can break it down in 2-3 months, but if you have heavy clay soil, you may still hit chunks of pumpkin a year from now, so be patient.

A healthy, mature Halloween pumpkin contains hundreds of plump seeds loaded with goodness. If your pumpkin grew with vibrant color and a firm rind, these seeds are prime candidates for saving for next year. Strain the tangled seed mass in a colander and massage it under a stream of cold running tap water to strip away the pulp. Spread the cleaned seeds in a single layer over non-stick parchment paper, a fine metal screen, or a ceramic plate. Let them dry in a warm, well-ventilated room out of direct sunlight for 2-3 weeks.

To test for dryness, try bending one: if it flexes, it still retains moisture, but if it snaps in half, your seeds are ready to store. Slide your dried seeds into breathable kraft paper seed envelopes. Pour them into paper seed envelopes, like the Seed Packet Kraft Envelopes, available from Walmart in packs of 100. Write the variety and date on the front, and store in a cool, dark drawer. Word to the wise, though: modern carving pumpkins are typically hybrids that won’t go true to type. Also, bees can cross-pollinate squash varieties across neighborhood zucchinis, so next spring’s seedlings may produce some wacky, unpredictable gourds.

Songbirds burn through vital fat stores as November temperatures drop, and a firm pumpkin makes a wonderful natural feeding bowl (although it’s best to stick to uncarved porch pumpkins for this project). Cut your pumpkin in half across the middle, or slice the top third off. Using a sturdy spoon or hori-hori to scrape out the inner pulp and seeds, until the interior walls are clean. Poke 3-4 half-inch (1.25cm) drainage holes through the base using a large screwdriver.

Punch 3 evenly spaced holes along the thick top rim, thread some sturdy jute twine through, and hang the bowl from a sturdy tree limb or pergola beam. Alternatively, set the flat shell on a low wall, tree stump, or deck railing. Fill with black-oil sunflower seeds or a good seed blend, such as Pennington Wild Bird Food from The Home Depot. You can also use some of your rinsed and dried pumpkin seeds as extra treats. These nutritious kitchen scraps make a nourishing treat for cardinals, blue jays and titmice. Just inspect every few days: when the inner walls turn squishy or develop fuzz, take the feeder down and consign it to the compost heap.

If you have a solid (again, uncarved) ornamental pumpkin on your porch, you can turn it into a temporary planter. Carve a generous opening around the stem and scoop out the pulp and seeds. Using a long screwdriver, puncture 4-5 generous drainage holes through the bottom crust. If you need a good screwdriver, Black Canyon’s Phillips Extended Length Screwdriver with Soft Grip Ergonomic Handle from Walmart is an efficient way to punch through thick rinds. Elevate the pumpkin on some stone or a trivet for drainage, as sitting water will rot the base rapidly.

Fill the lower half of the pumpkin with light, free-draining potting soil, then tuck in your choice of cold-tolerant fall ornamentals. Some great options include dwarf flowering kales, ruffled ornamental cabbages, winter violas, pansies, and trailing English ivy. These cold-hardy choices will look fresh and colorful for 2-4 weeks. With wet soil sitting inside it, the pumpkin starts softening from the inside out, and a few freeze-thaw nights will hurry it along. When yours starts to sag, move the plants to a bed or regular pot, and compost the gourd.

Slugs and garden snails are a persistent menace in fall, but at night they seek shelter in dark, damp, sheltered crevices to conserve moisture. A curved chunk of pumpkin rind provides a perfect natural decoy. Take sections of rind, including leftover pieces from carving or scraps that have softened too much for bird feeders. Place them skin-side up on the soil, beside vulnerable vegetable rows, hosta crowns, or mulched borders. The sweet scent of decaying squash flesh will attract slugs from several feet away, luring them under the hollowed domes.

Early the following morning, flip the rinds over. You should find dozens of slugs, snails, and earwigs clinging to the flesh. Scrape them off into a bucket of warm soapy water, or feed them to backyard chickens. Reset the traps for several nights in a row. Every slug removed now is one fewer laying eggs. Once the rind collapses, compost it. Dust a little Harris Food Grade Diatomaceous Earth Powder, available from Amazon, around your traps to stop slugs escaping back into your beds.

This last one is a lovely eco-friendly bonus for anyone keen to support overwintering beneficial insects in their yard. As fall frosts intensify, beneficial predatory insects and pollinators seek sheltered crevices. Ground beetles, centipedes, roving rove beetles, lacewings, lady bugs, and solitary native bees are valuable allies in the organic garden, consuming thousands of aphids, slug eggs, and weed seeds. You can turn a hollowed pumpkin shell into a cozy winter sanctuary. Take an uncarved or cleanly carved pumpkin. Slice a wide entryway near the base (or prop the shell upside-down on a couple of flat stones to leave an open gap underneath).

Stuff the cavity with natural textural materials that create micro-tunnels and air pockets. Use bundles of dry hollow plant stems, bamboo canes, small pine cones, crumpled dry leaves, and coarse straw. You can buy Bell Nursery Mini Straw Bales from The Home Depot which can also be used as mulch for strawberries and other overwintering plants. Tuck your bug hotel beneath a thick hedge, under a quiet shrub border, or along a perennial bed out of wind and rain. The shell will slowly soften, insulating the center. By spring, it will return harmlessly to the soil, leaving your beneficial guardians safely in the mulch bed, ready to go to work.

Before you drag your hollowed Halloween pumpkins down to the street corner, hopefully these ideas show you that they could be working hard for your yard. These seasonal gourds are far more than short-lived porch decorations. By turning into a rich soil ingredient, feeding wild birds, constructing cozy shelters for beneficial beetles and stocking up on seeds to plant next year’s pumpkins, you keep valuable resources out of landfills and grab a head start on next year's growth. Once winter sets in, those leftover gourds may already be enriching your soil: a true win-win!

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#7809. Is Your Dog Weird Enough for Times Square?

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Does your pup have a bedtime routine that makes no sense, a suspicious obsession with household objects, or dramatically howl at their own reflection in the oven door? Congratulations. You might be living with a contender for the World's Weirdest Dog. Embark Veterinary has officially launched its search for canine oddballs, inviting pet parents to submit photos and videos of their furballâs most gloriously bizarre behaviors before November 15, 2026. The winning pup will earn the ultimate claim to canine fame: their face on a Times Square billboard, the official title of World's Weirdest Dog, and a $200 gift card.

The contest celebrates the behaviors that make dogs funny, unique, and truly memorable; the ones that make us smile when we think about them, while also highlighting  Embark's Behavior Insights & Training feature, which explores how canine DNA may influence behavior.

Sock Thieves, Bathtub Sleepers, and Other Household Oddballs

Furry weirdos have interesting, different habits; Embark's examples include a dog who sleeps upside down in the bathtub, one who carries a sock around without chewing it, and a canine who spins exactly three times before lying down. Not two. Not four. Three.

Then there's the dog who refuses to walk past one particular house, or the dinner diva who won't touch a meal until someone has given it the full restaurant treatment.

Such behaviors are entertaining partly because they are so unique and specific. Most pet parents can share at least one story that would make a perfectly reasonable person wonder what goes on inside that furry little head.

A sock might be a very treasured object, a source of comfort, a reminder of their favorite personâs scent, or simply something fun to carry. A particular walking route might feel uncomfortable for reasons a person cannot detect, most likely a scentâ¦ but then again, who knows? And a bedtime ritual may have started with nothing more mysterious than finding a comfortable position.

Of course, some dogs are just little weirdos, and that's part of their charm. But there's a difference between a pup who has always slept with their legs in the air and one who suddenly starts acting strangely. If your pup begins staring at walls, repeating the same movements, or turning down food when that's not normal for them, don't automatically label it as a new amusing personality trait. Pain, illness, and anxiety can all show up as changes in behavior. If something feels off, put the camera down and call the vet.

Genes can influence behavioral tendencies, but they don't write a complete script for an individual dog's life. Learning and environment play a big role, too, sometimes in ways pet parents never intended.

Take the sock thief. A dog grabs a sock, their pet parents react with dramatic excitement, and suddenly the household is involved in a thrilling chase. From our perspective, it's a laundry crime. From the pup's perspective, it may be an excellent new game.

Behaviors that lead to positive or rewarding outcomes are more likely to happen again. Attention, play, food, and access to preferred activities can all reinforce behavior, even when nobody is training anything on purpose.

Genetics can contribute, too. Inherited tendencies may influence a dog's motivation to chase, retrieve, explore, or seek food. But a predisposition doesn't guarantee a particular behavior, nor does it explain every individual habit. A dog's behavior comes from a combination of biology and learned experience, which is often less convenient than blaming everything on their breed, but it is much closer to reality.

A 2022 study published in Science looked at the behavior and DNA of thousands of dogs. Researchers found that a dog's breed explained only about 9% of the differences in behavior between individual dogs. In other words, dogs of the same breed can have very different personalities and behaviors. Genetics plays a role, but it doesn't tell the whole story.

That doesn't mean genetics is irrelevant. The researchers found evidence that many behavioral traits do have a heritable component. Rather, the findings show why breed alone is a poor crystal ball for predicting how an individual dog will behave.

Some dogs may be especially motivated to retrieve, chase, or investigate, reflecting tendencies shaped partly by their ancestry and breeding history. But individual dogs still vary, and experience helps shape how those tendencies appear. However, with more data, we may learn new things; science is ever evolving along with our technologies.

Embark's Behavior Insights & Training feature connects genetic information with behavioral insights and training guidance. Genetic results can be useful, but they are one piece of the puzzle and not a personality prediction.

Behavior is best understood in context. Has the habit been present for years, or did it start last week? What happens before the behavior? Could pain, fear, stress, or another medical issue be contributing?

If a pup is safe and comfortable, there's often no reason to stop a peculiar routine unless itâs a problem. A dog who carries a favorite toy around the house doesn't need a corrective training plan. When a behavior does create a problem, redirection and positive reinforcement can help teach an alternative response without relying on intimidation or punishment. This is the science of behavioral modification.

The goal isn't to turn every pup into a perfectly polished obedience champion, but to help us understand what each dog needs and help them become great family members.

Flowerbuds should be forming by late fall but you'll need to get November Christmas cactus care right to enjoy a first-rate festive flower show.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

By November, your Christmas cactus should be busy preparing to flower, and what you do with your plant now is the difference between a disappointing bud-drop or a dazzling display of festive flowers. We think of cacti as being easy plants to grow but the Christmas cactus is a rather sensitive soul. Native to the coastal rainforests of Brazil, Shlumbergera x buckleyi can struggle to flower well in the very different environment of our homes, and even jettison all its buds.

Get November Christmas cactus care right, however, and you’ll have a happy plant in full, fabulous bloom for the holidays. What's more, stick to these guidelines and those flowers will last for longer, even brightening the first few weeks of the new year.

The four principles of caring for a Christmas cactus in late fall are super-simple to achieve, and knowing exactly what your plant needs to stay focused on swelling those precious buds changes everything. Here's what to do to stop a Christmas cactus dropping its buds so you can enjoy weeks of fabulous flowers right through the holidays.

In November, your Christmas cactus should be setting buds so check regularly for tiny pinpricks of color on the leaf tips. These nubs will be bright red, pink or purple or, if you have a white-flowering variety, a very pale green, so they’re easy to spot.

If you’ve been using light and dark to trick your Christmas cactus into flowering right on time for the holidays, you’ll very likely spot plenty of these baby flowerbuds in mid-November. If you haven’t, don’t panic, because you may still get Christmas cactus flowers this winter. Your Shlumbergera may well have set flowerbuds without any extra encouragement from you, especially if its natural seasonal cues haven't been interrupted by artificial evening light or too much warmth or water.

If you're trying the light and dark trick, carry on until you spot buds. If not, and there’s no sign of buds yet, move your cactus to a cool room that’s not often used so lights aren’t routinely switched on – a spare bedroom is ideal. Turn the radiator down and leave the blind or curtains open so the air naturally cools at night to 50-55°F – a cheap indoor thermometer such as this from Amazon makes it easy to check. Only water the cactus sparsely once the top 2-3 inches of soil feel dry, as drought conditions can trigger flowering, and keep your fingers crossed!

As soon as you spot buds, move your Christmas cactus to a spot that gets bright, indirect sunlight and the temperature stays around 65-70°F. You can give your plant a little more water now, too, irrigating when the top inch of soil feels dry or take out the guesswork with a moisture meter such as this long-probe soil meter from Amazon. Aim to keep the soil consistently just-damp.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

The dry air of a heated home is a far cry from a Christmas cactus’ natural environment of a moist rainforest , and this is a real threat to the holiday flowers. When the heat is first turned on, the shock is a common reason why Christmas cacti drop a leaf segment. And if the too-dry conditions continue, a cactus can lose so much moisture from its stems that it goes into survival mode and, because those developing flowers are using a heap of energy, jettisons its buds.

Setting your plant on a humidity tray is a quick and easy answer. A bonsai pebble tray such as this from Lowe’s is perfect, or make your own with a plant saucer and pea gravel pebbles like this Landscape Rock from The Home Depot. Add water to the tray but sit the plant pot on the pebbles so its base is above the water level: the water will then naturally evaporate, increasing air humidity for your houseplant, rather than being drawn up into the potting soil. Keeping the tray topped up with water will also help flowers last for longer once they open.

As well as being very sensitive to the level of moisture in the air, your Christmas cactus will respond negatively to any other changes in its environment. So, if you want those flowerbeds to swell right on schedule, you must leave your plant in the same spot.

In the rainforest beneath a dense tree canopy, the buds of Shlumbergera lock onto whichever direction precious sunlight comes from. So, if you move the cactus, those buds will likely twist towards the changed light source and drop off. Any change in temperature can also trigger bud drop – and your cactus is so reactive, it’ll notice being moved to another table, not just a different room.

You have until the flowerbuds start to form a teardrop shape or reach around ¼ inch long to decide where you want your cactus to sit until after it’s finished flowering, but then leave it be. Don’t even rotate it a half inch! It's even worth making a pencil mark on the pot and on the surface it sits on so you can line them back up if the pot gets knocked. If there’s not enough natural light in the spot you’d like it, then a basic dimmable LED grow light such as this from Walmart is the answer.

Now you know exactly what to do with a Christmas cactus in November to keep it happy and healthy. It takes around 4-6 weeks for buds to grow from those tiny pinpricks you first spotted into flamboyant flowers with flared petals, so there's still plenty of time to get festive blooms in time for the holidays. Just give your Shlumbergera the correct soil moisture, the humidity it craves and the stability it needs, and your plant will reward you with a phenomenal show. With each flower lasting up to 9 days and buds continuing to open over a few weeks, your plant's blooming period will last for at least a month, so you'll have plenty of time to enjoy the festive flowers.

#7806. Lights Out, Zoomies On: Why Dogs Go Wild at Bedtime

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

While nighttime zoomies are a well-recognized phenomenon in the feline world, it turns out dogs can also get a little over-excited at the prospect of bedtime. Just as the house is settling down for the night, a dog may start bouncing around, digging into the blankets, or demanding attention.

It also turns out that there isn't a single explanation for this evening burst of energy; there are several. The bed itself can be exciting, particularly because it smells like a favorite person and offers a chance for interaction. In other cases, a dog may simply have energy left to burn. Understanding the possible reasons can help explain why bedtime sometimes turns into playtime.

Dogs spend much of their time looking up at people from the floor. Climbing onto a bed changes that perspective, bringing a dog much closer to its owner's face and making interaction easier.

That alone can be enough to spark a playful mood. A dog may drop into a play bow, bark for attention, or bounce around in an attempt to encourage its person to join in.

Being face to face can make play feel more inviting, particularly for dogs that enjoy close interaction with their owners. What looks like a sudden burst of energy may simply be a dog making the most of the opportunity to engage on a different level.

A bed carries the scent of the person who sleeps in it, making it an especially interesting place for a dog to explore. Dogs rely heavily on their noses to understand their surroundings, and familiar smells can be particularly appealing.

For a dog that enjoys spending time with its owner, the bed may be one of the most comforting and interesting places in the home. Rolling around on the sheets or sniffing the blankets lets a dog investigate those familiar scents while enjoying a spot associated with its favorite person.

That combination of comfort, familiarity, and excitement can help explain why some dogs become especially playful once they climb onto the mattress.

For dogs that love burrowing, a bed covered in sheets and blankets can feel like an invitation to play. Digging, wriggling underneath the covers, and pushing through folds of fabric can all become part of the fun.

Some breeds are particularly inclined toward this kind of behavior. Dachshunds, for example, were bred to pursue animals such as badgers and weasels into their burrows. Their instinct to dig and tunnel can make a pile of blankets especially appealing. Meanwhile, Chihuahuas seem to be particularly fond of burrowing into the warmth and security of their humanâs bed.

A dog that discovers the pleasure of diving between the sheets may quickly turn it into a regular bedtime activity.

Dogs are often quick to learn which behaviors get a reaction from their owners. Climbing onto the bed puts them right where they're difficult to ignore, particularly if they start bouncing around or nudging someone for attention.

Bedtime can also signal that the day is winding down and an opportunity for cuddling is approaching. A dog that enjoys being close to its owner may become excited at the prospect of spending that time together.

If playful behavior consistently earns attention, a dog may be encouraged to repeat it. What begins as a burst of excitement can become a familiar part of the nightly routine. Even if this nightly ritual isnât one you welcome, waving arms and raised voices often count as a positive interaction for a dog, so if youâre trying to get your dog off the bed, be careful your methods align with your message.

Sometimes, a dog becomes especially energetic at bedtime simply because theyâre not ready to settle down. If it hasn't had enough exercise or stimulation during the day, the bed may become an outlet for that leftover energy.

A dog that is still eager to run, jump, and play may need more activity before the household turns in for the night. An evening walk or a game of tug-of-war can help provide an opportunity to burn off some energy before bedtime.

A dog that's had enough exercise and stimulation is more likely to be ready to relax, rather than treating the mattress as a playground.

Many owners enjoy sleeping alongside their dogs, while others prefer to keep their beds pet-free. Sharing a bed can feel cozy and comforting, and having a dog nearby may also be soothing for people who experience anxiety or other mental health challenges.

There are practical considerations, too. Dogs can carry dirt, bacteria, and parasites into the bed, and some owners would rather not have fur on their sheets or pillows.

Ultimately, whether a dog is allowed to sleep on the bed comes down to what works for the household. If itâs not a problem, then itâs not a problem. There's no single right choice, and a dog can still enjoy plenty of affection and companionship without sharing the mattress.

If you do want your bed to be a dog-free zone, the simplest solution is to keep the bedroom door closed. But if youâre simply looking for a way to get them off the bed without it turning into a party, a calm and quiet approach is best. A single command or using a slip-lead to silently guide them off the bed will be far more effective than shouting and pointing.

A dog getting frisky on the bed is often responding to a combination of familiar scents, opportunities for attention, and the chance to play somewhere comfortable. Blankets can add to the appeal, especially for dogs that enjoy burrowing.

If the behavior seems excessive, however, it may be worth looking at how much exercise and stimulation the dog gets during the day. Adding a walk or play session before bed can help make the transition to sleep easier.

For many dogs, the bed is simply an exciting place to be close to their favorite person. With a little preparation, bedtime can still end in a peaceful night's sleep rather than an impromptu wrestling match.

Is it legal for a neighbor to film your backyard? Sadly, the answer to this question is a bit wishy-washy: it depends. Like many of the issues I tackle in my Gardening Lawyer series, the legality of this kind of neighborhood surveillance depends on state and local laws, what the camera captures, and how it’s being used. Read on to find out what to do.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

All cameras “see,” but some also “hear.” Does the fact that a surveillance camera also records sound impact its legality? It definitely can.

If the neighbor’s camera has a microphone, you may have another layer of legal protection. Rules about recording are separate and apart from rules about filming. Have you heard of wiretapping laws? Well, they can apply to surveillance camera audio. Just because the filming may be legal doesn’t mean capturing conversations is.

This is a federal issue that is determined under the terms of the federal Wiretap Act. It provides that unless a recording is taken as part of a criminal or civil investigation, at least one of the people whose private conversation is being recorded must give consent to the recording. The neighbor with the camera is not considered part of the conversation, and therefore cannot give that consent.

And that’s just a base level of protection. I live in California, and it is among the states that impose even stricter requirements for consent to recording conversations. The state Penal Code requires that all parties to a confidential conversation consent, although the statute includes a few exceptions.

The law rarely offers a clear litmus test for when a crime is committed. Think about it. Even killing someone is not a crime in some situations. So it’s no surprise that the question of when surveillance becomes harassment involves a weighing of relevant factors.

You need to know your local laws in order to move forward if your neighbor decides not to accommodate your concerns. Check your city laws and state laws. If you are part of an HOA, check the CC&Rs (Covenants, Conditions, and Restrictions). Speak with an attorney if necessary to figure out your rights.

If you decide you want to take the matter to law enforcement or the courts, start documenting the surveillance and all written communications between you. This material will be helpful if you decide to file a police report or a civil claim against them.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

The season may be winding down but there’s plenty you can do now to protect those tubers so your dahlias come back stronger next summer. These 5 secrets unlock your best blooms ever

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The first fall frosts bring a dramatic and abrupt curtain call to flower borders. And for any dahlias that might have been bursting with dinner-plate blooms just days earlier, it can come as a bit of a shock when freezing temperatures leave them limp and shriveled. For new dahlia growers, this sudden collapse can be devastating. Yet while the stems and leaves may be wilting and the flowers may be done, the tubers remain very much alive and capable of producing decades of future blooms.

So take heart, because you can enjoy those gorgeous displays again, as long as you take the right steps now. The days following first frosts are critical if these tubers are to push new growth out next year. These Mexican and Central American natives need care in order to see out the next few months. If these tubers are subjected to hard-frozen subsoil or waterlogged winter mud, they might easily rot and perish.

To keep your favorite cultivars thriving year after year, you need to decide how to overwinter dahlias, either by lifting the tubers for indoor storage or by applying the right protection and insulation in milder regions. The right approach depends on your regional hardiness zone, local soil drainage, and weather. While it might be a little daunting at first, getting your dahlias ready for winter is a relatively simple process. Whether you lift or leave in the ground, here’s how to prime your dahlias for winter.

Timing is key if you want your dahlia tubers to survive winter, and it’s vital to pay heed to your USDA hardiness zone to help your dahlia tubers to survive winter. Never dig your dahlias before the initial frost. That frost sends a biochemical signal through the plant, letting it know that the growing season has ended. In response, the plant channels its remaining energy down into the ground, plumping up the tubers in preparation for dormancy. So allowing the blackened stems to rest untouched for a week or so after this frost ensures the tubers reach peak maturity.

Your overwintering choices will depend on where you live. If you are in zones 6 and colder, it’s best to lift tubers every fall. Winter ground freezes in these latitudes can be lethal for unprotected tubers. Zone 7 gardens are borderline: lifting is still advised, but tubers in sandy, well-draining soil can survive beneath heavy insulation. In mild southern and coastal regions (zones 8-11), many dahlia varieties can remain safely in the ground, provided winter soil drains freely and the tubers have some protection.

You don’t have to remove the tubers right after the first frost. Let the foliage die back naturally. Any green foliage is still collecting energy to store in the tubers. You don’t want to disrupt that process prematurely. However, if you are in a very cold climate where the ground is going to freeze before the foliage has died, don’t wait. Keep an eye on the weather forecast to decide when to dig and lift your tubers. The goal is to let them mature without freezing them. In warmer climates, you have more flexibility.

Before you start, check the soil with a soil meter like the Raintrip 4-in-1 Soil Meter from Amazon. This will help you determine when the ground is nearing that freezing threshold ahead of lifting or mulching. Dahlia type and variety matter, too. Massive dinner plate varieties (such as Café au Lait) produce heavy tuber clumps that require longer drying times, whereas compact varieties (like the Gallery series) form tight root balls that dry quickly. Whichever area and variety you have, these steps will help you to ensure your dahlias return with a bang next summer…

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

The first step is to cut back stems and foliage. Once the foliage has blackened and you have allowed the root system a week to absorb its final starches, you’re ready. Using sharp bypass pruners, sever the main stalks down to 4-6 inches (10-15cm). If you are after a pair of bypass pruners, the Corona BP Dual Link Bypass Pruners from Amazon are perfect for slicing through the thick stalks in a single pass without crushing vital tissue.

Leaving short, sturdy stems is vital, as it gives you a safe gripping point for lifting the heavy tuber clusters and reduces pressure on delicate tuber necks. You can also use them to attach identifying labels. Just make sure that you cut the stalks just before lifting. Dahlia stalks are hollow, so if you cut stems down and leave them through days of heavy rain, water will pool around the tuber and trigger rot. Cut on a dry morning and plan to lift tubers the same day to keep water from causing problems.

Now, you’re ready to lift your tubers, but do it slowly and carefully. The tuberous roots and the narrow neck that connects them to the crown can break easily. If these necks snap, twist, or crack during digging, the tuber becomes useless. Use a garden fork to dig several inches around the plant. Get under the roots with the fork, inserting the tines 10-12 inches (25-30cm) away from the main stem. Rock the fork handle backward to loosen the soil, working in a full circle around the plant.

Gently lift the clump, using the shortened stems to help, but don’t yank hard on the stalk. Once lifted, gently shake away loose clods of earth. Inspect the roots, and snip away any soft, mushy, or damaged tubers. However, resist dividing the tubers now. Those cuts can leave them vulnerable to rot or infections in winter storage. You can add a little sulfur power such as Bonide Sulfur Plant Fungicide Dust from Walmart to stems to prevent storage rots. Alternatively, dust stem cuts with a little cinnamon.

Your tubers will need a little time to dry before being packed away. Place them upside down on slatted wooden trays, wire screens, or newspaper in a shaded, frost-free, well-ventilated space at 55-65°F (13-18°C). Let the clumps dry for 2-3 days until the skin feels dry and leathery. But don’t leave them so long that the tubers begin to wrinkle or shrivel.

Pack the dry tubers in breathable containers, such as cardboard boxes, wooden apple crates, or plastic storage totes with the lids cracked open. Nestle the tubers in a sterile, moisture-buffering medium, such as dry vermiculite, horticultural perlite, coarse wood shavings, or peat-free coir. You can buy Miracle-Gro Perlite from The Home Depot to help cushion dormant tubers while absorbing excess humidity to prevent winter mold. Make sure individual tubers do not touch.

Move your container into a dark, unheated room, such as a cellar, basement corner, or frost-free garage. Make sure it holds steady at 40-50°F (4-10°C). Stored tubers need a balance of moisture and dryness. Check on the tubers a few times over winter. If they are too moist, repack in drier material. If too dry, give them a light spritz of water.

If you are in zones 8-11 (or a sheltered microclimate in zone 7), you can overwinter your dahlia tubers in the ground. However, success depends on 3 factors: mild winters, excellent winter soil drainage, and insulation. Heavy clay soil that stays saturated in winter will rot tubers in the ground, regardless of ambient air warmth. Wait for the first frost to blacken the leaves, then cut the stalks down to 2-3 inches (5-8cm). Immediately cap the hollow stem ends with small inverted plastic cups, foil wraps, or a dab of horticultural wax to prevent rain from channeling into the crowns.

After cutting back dead stems, spread a generous 4-6-inch (10-15cm) blanket of loose, organic mulch over the surface. Try team favorite Back to the Roots Organic Premium Mulch from Amazon for a lush bark mulch that insulates from freeze-thaw cycles and suppresses weeds. You can also use clean agricultural straw or chopped dry leaves for protection against cold snaps, while helping to maintain healthy soil aeration.

Container-grown dahlias are vulnerable to freeze-thaw shocks. Left on an exposed patio, tubers can turn to ice in hours, while ceramic and terracotta planters are prone to cracking. It’s wise to move the container to a sheltered location for winter. Just be sure the soil will stay dry and the storage area won’t freeze. Once frost kills foliage, cut the stalks back to 4 inches (10cm), cease watering, and allow the potting mix to dry out. In colder regions, move the pot to an unheated garage, shed, or basement where temperatures are 35-45°F (2-7°C). If indoor space is unavailable in borderline zones, cluster containers tightly against a sheltered, south-facing foundation wall.

Wrap the containers in heavy layers of burlap or thermal bubble wrap, and mound loose straw over the top of the soil as a light mulch layer. Sta-Green Burlap Blankets from Lowe’s are a great breathable option for insulating grouped containers against winter winds and chills. Alternatively, you can lift and store tubers, just as with in-ground dahlias. Unpot the root ball, gently tease away the potting mix, and store the bare tubers in crates of vermiculite, just as you would for in-ground tubers.

Just because this season is over, that doesn’t mean you can’t enjoy your dahlias again. A little extra effort now allows you to enjoy these gorgeous blooms year after year. Caring for your dahlias after the first fall frosts doesn’t require special techniques or time-intensive labor. A half hour is all you need to cut back frost-nipped stalks, lever tuber clumps from the earth, and pack them into cozy quarters, or protect them if you leave them where they are. If you do tuck your tubers away this month, you just need to check in on them occasionally over winter Next year, your tubers will be in great shape and fully primed to deliver your most breathtaking blooms yet.

My professional gardener husband knows better than anyone that roses need a little extra attention before winter arrives...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

What do roses need in November? As the wife of a professional gardener, I’ve learned that there are just three things these beloved flowers crave from us.

Now, my husband has spent more than 20 years caring for gardens, and he has always had roses (more specifically, hybrid roses) on his unofficial list of plants that he will never let me buy, no matter how much I might beg and plead with him over the matter. That's not to say, though, that he doesn't know how to care for them; he has looked after plenty of these thorny flowers over the past two decades.

So, if you want to keep your own blooming beauties safe during extreme low temperatures and even occasional thaws, look this way...

I love my roses to bits (because yes, I still have a few in my garden – I've just made sure to stick to tougher, more wildlife-friendly roses like Rosa rugosa), but every winter I turn to my husband with wide and pleading eyes whenever the forecast starts muttering about "the big freeze".

Thankfully, his advice is always the same (and always so calmly delivered), and it all hinges on three easy tasks...

My husband's first tip for prepping roses in November is simple enough: look for tall and unruly rose canes. While he never gives his roses a major pruning in November, he does shorten any excessively long growth that could be whipped around by strong winter winds.

"High wind can catch tall growth, violently rocking the plant back and forth in the ground," he explains. "This loosens and tears the root system, often creating a gap at the base where water can pool, freeze, and rot the roots."

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Just remember that this is a protective trim, not an opportunity to reshape the entire bush. Save your main structural pruning for late winter or early spring, when the worst of the cold weather has passed.

"Don't leave that mess sitting around the bottom of your roses. You'll only regret it come spring." This is one adage my husband is particularly strict about, and he always works to remove fallen leaves from around the base of every rose in November – and picks off any diseased foliage still clinging to the stems, too.

The reason? Fungal diseases such as black spot, rust, and powdery mildew can survive on infected plant material, potentially causing problems when warmer, wetter weather returns. "It's much easier to clean it up now than deal with another outbreak next year," he says.

As ever, he's right (although don't tell him I said so). Removing infected foliage and disposing of it appropriately helps reduce the amount of disease-carrying material left around the plants over winter.

"Mulch is your best friend in winter. Never underestimate it."

I know I've heard this a thousand times, but my husband really does swear by it. In colder regions, he recommends making like Martha Stewart when it comes to winterizing roses in November: think mounding mulch around the base of vulnerable roses to protect the crown and graft union from freezing temperatures.

Repeated freezing and thawing can damage exposed roots and even push plants out of the ground. A protective mound, though? Why, that helps insulate these vulnerable areas against temperature fluctuations.

"Just make sure you're protecting the important bit," he tells me. "And don't assume every rose needs the same treatment."

And... well, that's it! "People think roses are difficult," my husband often says, "but most problems start when you don't give them the attention they need."

Honestly, after watching him care for roses year after year? I have to agree. A few simple jobs in November can make all the difference when those first spring shoots appear... even if that just looks like treating yourself to a few new bare root plants and getting them in the ground.

Hey, you deserve a garden full of roses – even if I'm not allowed!
