#7754. Discovery Sanctions Recommended in "Are You a Jew? … Are You a Zionist?" Case

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The factual allegations, from a Sept. 2025 decision in the case by Judge Susan Illston (N.D. Cal.) (the case is Radice v. Jerusalem Boxing Club, LLC consolidated with the federal government's U.S. v. Harara):

The Jerusalem Coffee House [which Harara owns] is a business establishment open to the general public. The coffee house is located on the premises of the East Bay Community Space, "which regularly hosts events that are open to the general public for exhibition or entertainment …."

According to the complaint, on June 10, 2024, Michael Radice—who is Jewish—went to the East Bay Community Space "for the purpose of viewing the establishment for a fundraising event for his organization." Radice was wearing a dark blue baseball cap with a light blue Star of David and white Hebrew lettering. As he approached the community space from the side where the coffee house is located, a man sitting at a table in front of the coffee house asked, "Are you a Jew?" Radice answered in the affirmative. The man then asked, "Are you a Zionist?" Radice declined to respond.

The complaint alleges that "[t]he man then began shouting numerous accusations at Mr. Radice, including that he was complicit in Israel's military actions in the Gaza Strip following the October 7, 2023 Hamas attacks and guilty of 'killing children.'" As Radice began to walk away, the man stood up and asked, "Where are you going?" The complaint alleges, "Mr. Radice saw another man, whom he later learned was Harara, walk out of the coffee house and speak to the man, and the two went inside." …

And now from Judge Thomas Hixson's Report and Recommendation yesterday:

There is no dispute that Defendant Abdulrahim Harara violated at least six discovery orders. Motion at 4-7 ("Harara has flouted at least six discovery orders," and enumerating the violations); Opp. at 7 ("But the question on this motion is not whether any order was violated; it is whether the record as a whole shows the kind of deliberate, deceptive obstruction that makes a fair trial impossible and justifies ending the case without one.")….

The real issue is what remedy the Court should impose for the serial violations of its discovery orders. The impact of Harara's conduct basically falls into three buckets: documents were produced late that should have been produced earlier; some document productions are incomplete; and there has been a wholesale failure to produce email. But having reviewed the voluminous evidence submitted in support of Radice's motion for sanctions, the Court thinks truth is available to the parties, and they should go ahead and have a trial on the existing record.

Harara's biggest failure in discovery is the nonproduction of email, and he does not have a good excuse. In many cases the total failure to produce email would justify terminating sanctions or at least adverse inference instructions.

But the Court is skeptical that this is such a case. The relevant events are alleged in-person refusals to serve Radice and another individual because they are Jewish. In other words, the relevant events did not occur by email. Before email existed, public accommodation discrimination claims like this were tried the old fashioned way: The participants in the alleged events testified, and the trier of fact decided who to believe. That option is still available here.

Email is still relevant, of course, because it could contain statements about what happened, or have evidence of the defendant's allegedly prejudicial intent. But here a lot of that type of evidence was produced in the form of Harara's text messages and social media feeds and other electronic records. These include a statement that seems to be by Harara that seems to say he throws pennies on the ground when Jews walk by; the coffee shop menu and outdoor signage with inverted red triangles, which Radice alleges is a symbol used by Hamas to mark Israeli targets in propaganda videos; the apparent introduction on the one year anniversary of the October 7 attack of a juice item named for a mastermind of the attack; a video of Harara telling a Jewish customer to leave because he had "a violent hat," referring to the Star of David on the hat; and a repost by Harara to his X account bearing the "Bay Area" screen name of a November 2, 2024 post calling that same Jewish customer "a genocidal, bottom dwelling Zionist scum" who "should be kicked out of every public establishment not just Palestinian owned ones!" There are also text messages that replicate the kind of thing a plaintiff would dream of finding in a defendant's emails—and certainly at trial Radice and the United States will argue these texts are strong evidence of liability.

Radice is certainly of the view that he has uncovered good evidence, even if it was produced later than it should have been, and even though it does not include email. See Motion at 15 ("The 6134 Bates-labeled pages and 2474 native files that Harara produced on or after August 7 include inflammatory documents that Harara willfully withheld until after discovery closed."); id. ("For example, a January 3, 2025 JCH Instagram post shows JCH advertising for sale a t-shirt featuring the Jerusalem Coffee House name ringed by flags with the emblem of Hamas, a designated terrorist organization dedicated to violence against Jews and Israelis."); id. ("His Instagram direct-messages contain both antisemitic tropes and antisemitic slurs.").

With all this evidence, can it really be said that Harara's failings in discovery have prejudiced Plaintiffs to such an extent that a meaningful and fair trial is no longer possible? That adverse inferences are needed because there is not enough evidence for the trier of fact to reliably draw conclusions about what happened?

No. These cases are about whether a coffee shop committed discrimination, and Harara has produced enough documents that Radice and the United States have what they need to go to trial. Even with the nonproduction of email, it is not true that discovery failed or that truth cannot be ascertained. The public policy in favor of deciding cases on the merits applies here.

Accordingly, the Court RECOMMENDS that the district judge DENY the request for terminating sanctions because there's just no need or basis for it. The Court DENIES the request for adverse inferences because it is essentially a request for a directed verdict. Each side should put on their case at trial, and truth should be determined in the normal way. There is no reason for the Court to stack the deck.

But that doesn't mean Harara escapes sanctions. He needs to pay for what he did. His serial violations of Court orders significantly drove up Radice's cost of litigating [the case]. Radice requests $166,500.50 against all Defendants. The entity Defendants have been in default during the period of time when Harara violated the Court orders, so are not the cause of Radice's increased legal expenses, and therefore will not be sanctioned.

Plaintiff's counsel's rates are reasonable. However, both the Benesch and ADL attorneys seek fees for work that preceded the violations of the Court orders, a problem that requires deducting about a third of the Benesch time and about a fifth of the ADL's time. That brings the total down to $118,000. In addition, even though Harara violated multiple discovery orders, it is also true that Plaintiff's counsel litigated [the case] with excessive ferocity. At times it seemed they were not just litigating a discrimination case but were out to destroy Harara. As a result their fees were excessive. The Court estimates that about half of the fees Radice incurred during the time when Harara was violating the discovery orders was due to the violations and the other half was for work that would have needed to be done anyway or that should not have been done at all because it was excessive. Accordingly, the Court SANCTIONS Harara in the amount of $59,000 and ORDERS him to pay that amount to Radice within 30 days.

In his opposition, Harara proposes some remedial measures. However, the Court will not adopt any of them. The proposal to remedy the lack of email production presupposes that Harara will have a lawyer to represent him. Opp. at 16 ("The full inbox Mr. Harara exported on September 3, 2026 will be reviewed by counsel, consistent with the Court's ruling that counsel rather than Mr. Harara conduct that review. That counsel will be either counsel Mr. Harara retains or volunteer limited-scope counsel appointed through the Court's Federal Pro Bono Project under General Order 25, to which Mr. Harara respectfully requests referral. Since his counsel withdrew, Mr. Harara has contacted lawyers and legal organizations and has not found a lawyer who will take his case."). However, Harara's inability to work cooperatively with two sets of counsel means this is an unrealistic proposal. And if no lawyer represents him, Harara's proposal contains no particular deadline by which emails would be produced. Opp. at 16 ("If counsel has not been retained or appointed within 30 days of the Court's order, Mr. Harara will file a status report every 14 days thereafter. In all events, the production under this paragraph will be complete within 90 days of the Court's order; if it is not, Mr. Harara will show cause why not, and the Court may then impose such further measures as it finds appropriate after notice and an opportunity to be heard.").

Harara's proposal to serve further interrogatory responses is highly unlikely to achieve anything. And there is no need for a further deposition of him; Plaintiffs' counsel can cross-examine him at trial….

NEXT: 10-Year "Harassment"/"Stalking" Sentence for Repeatedly Criticizing Police Detective Violated First Amendment, Amicus Brief Argues

#7753. Amicus Brief in OneTaste Criminal Prosecution

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Matt Kezhaya (Kezhaya Law PLC) wrote an amicus brief on my behalf in this case (U.S. v. Cherwitz & Daedone) a few weeks ago—many thanks to him for all his work on it!—and I thought I'd pass it along:

Under the Government's theory of spiritual coercion, people who at one point believed that volunteering for a religious organization is the path to enlightenment or salvation, but who later become disillusioned with their former beliefs, can be found to have been retroactively "coerced" into providing that labor. The same logic could apply to nuns who had felt religious pressure to do the educational or nursing work that their order was known for, or to monks who had felt religious pressure to do agricultural work that supports the monastery. Any religious organization that runs a monastery, convent, or any other institution where adherents are expected to work as part of their religious vocation could likewise face felony prosecutions.

Such a theory of criminal liability violates the Free Exercise Clause because it is not "neutral." Governments depart from neutrality not just when legislators pass laws designed to suppress religion, but also when courts enforce otherwise-neutral laws in ways that suppress religion precisely because of spiritual or religious qualities. Liability in this case turned precisely on the religious nature of the allegedly coercive conduct, and was imposed in the absence of any secular coercion such as violence or the threat of violence.

The sexual subject matter and conduct inherent within OneTaste's beliefs and practices is beside the point. The forced labor statute is not limited to sexual labor. 18 U.S.C. § 1589. Rather, it generally prohibits any "labor" obtained through "threats of serious harm." 18 U.S.C. § 1589(a)(3). Indeed, the "labor" subject of this charge was ordinary, non-sexual administrative work entailed in running a religious organization that features events and communal living.

To be sure, laws that restrict sexual labor will usually be neutral and generally applicable, precisely because they do not turn on any claims of religious or spiritual coercion. If any business, religious or not, offers its employees' sexual services in exchange for money, that might well violate generally applicable bans on prostitution or pandering. Likewise, if any business, religious or not, conditions employment on the employee's performing sexual services, that will usually constitute civilly actionable quid pro quo sexual harassment. And enforcing such laws would not jeopardize ordinary religious labor, precisely because they are focused on a narrow range of secularly-defined behavior that is seen as harmful (the exchange of sex for money or employment) rather than on a theory of spiritual coercion that can apply to a wide range of labor.

But such laws were not used in this case. The essence of this charge was punishing a particular religious group. The Court should vacate the convictions, or at least reverse and remand for a new trial with proper limiting instructions.

[I.] A theory of "spiritual coercion" violates the Free Exercise Clause.

The Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment prohibits governments from targeting specific religious beliefs or practices as such. Church of Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah, 508 U.S. 520 (1993). That prohibition bars more than just legislative enactments expressly targeting religion; it extends to criminal prosecutions that apply facially neutral laws in ways that target disfavored religious beliefs. Fowler v. State of R.I., 345 U.S. 67 (1953).

Of course, as Part III will discuss, "neutral" and "generally applicable" criminal statutes may be applied to religious behavior precisely the same way they are applied to secular behavior; otherwise, each of us would "become a law unto himself." Emp. Div., Dep't of Hum. Res. of Oregon v. Smith, 494 U.S. 872, 885 (1990); see also Reynolds v. United States, 98 U.S. 145, 167 (1878). But this power cannot be used to target religious actions because of their religious or spiritual character.

The threshold inquiry is whether the ideas are, within OneTaste's scheme of things, "religious." See Patrick v. LeFevre, 745 F.2d 153, 158-59 (2d Cir. 1984). Indisputably, Defendants, OneTaste, and adherents of OneTaste (including the so-called victims) all considered the doctrines subject of this criminal trial to be "religious." See A-977 ("We believed that … your path to God was through your orgasm") (emphasis added); see also A-1053 (adherents of OneTaste seek "something more" beyond ordinary existence believe "Our most potent biological drive, Orgasm, is the key to unlocking this power.").

OneTaste's doctrines addressed distinctions between the physical and spiritual realms in a dichotomy between the "third dimension" and the "fourth dimension." See A-694. They addressed issues of worldly suffering and promised both enlightenment and transcendence through ceremonial rites. A-1114 (orgasm "was more about energy," borrowing from "Buddhist principles like the concept of qi"); see also A-1446 ("OneTaste teachings integrate the principles of mindfulness with the practice of orgasm"); A-1089 (OneTaste teachings included sex "as a ritual practice" and "Magic School … where we had sort of like priests and priestesses of orgasm"); see also A-1426-1427 (PowerPoint presentation outlining "Alchemize shadow into power through orgasm" and "Orgasm Magic: Bringing out the elements of magic [and] Put the principles of OM into practice in creating what you want … [including] Rituals and ceremonies"). Specific ceremonies described in the record include a marriage ceremony at A-891, a foot soaking ritual at A-1085, and a shower ritual at A-1152. The central ritual tenet of OneTaste was ritualistic sexual activity is, OMing, or "Orgasmic Meditation," which adherents of OneTaste regard as a mindfulness practice, a "meditation on sensation without a goal," A-577, A-785.

The Government made much of the sexual nature of those beliefs and practices. E.g., A-1229. But it is no business of the government, including the courts, to "prescribe what shall be orthodox in … religion." W. Virginia State Bd. of Educ. v. Barnette, 319 U.S. 624, 642 (1943). Because OneTaste and its adherents considered these beliefs and practices to be "religious" within their scheme of things, the Free Exercise Clause protects their beliefs and practices from governmental targeting.

And the Government did not seriously contest OneTaste's religiosity; instead, it acknowledged, and even stressed, the spiritual and religious nature of OneTaste's activities. According to the Government's closing arguments, the essence of the charge was that "the defendants indoctrinated the victims to believe that Nicole Daedone was a guru and that her teachings were the path to enlightenment and spiritual growth." A-1222. Prosecutors took issue that "Nicole Daedone taught that orgasm was God." A-1232. And "[n]early all of them [victims] lived in OneTaste housing and were subjected to these teachings incessantly." A-1234. The complained-of "indoctrination" and "teachings" is the very essence of religion: leading adherents to accept doctrines as spiritual truths. That these supposed victims ordered their lives in accordance with OneTaste's beliefs and practices is evidence of spiritual and religious belief, not of criminally punishable coercion.

Had there been evidence these "victims" were physically coerced into accepting OneTaste's religious doctrines, such physical coercion would certainly have been illegal. But that was not the Government's theory. Each of these so-called victims freely admitted that they voluntarily joined the organization. A-267-268; A-872-873; A-939; A-1152-1153. And they freely admitted that they voluntarily left it. A-882; A-939; A-1107. The "indoctrination" and "teachings" for which Defendants stood trial only describes proselytization, the very essence of religion, which cannot be criminally punished.

Likewise, the prosecution argued that Defendants "disrupted victims' personal relationships and isolated them from their friends and family." A-1222; see also A-1235 (victims "felt like OneTaste was all they had"). More particularly, Defendants did so by encouraging some of their adherents, including these "victims," to live in a commune with other like-minded believers. A-262, 359-60, 775, 893-894, 1004-06. But this disruption likewise stemmed not from physical coercion or threats of violence, of deportation, or of other secular harm. Rather, it stemmed from the adherents' sense of the spiritual value of participating in a particular religious and spiritual community. A-872; A-1008-1009 (Ms. Kandell, particularly, described her time at the commune as "one of the greatest experiences of my life," partly because of "the sense of community" and "the focus of the communal living"); A-1138-1139.

This is a commonplace practice among many religious orders. By definition, any follower of any monastic tradition could be described as having their personal relationships "disrupted" or becoming "isolated" from their less committed friends and family. Volokh, Addiction, 75 Emory L. J. at 1190. Nor does it say anything that a religion discourages association with non-adherents, as many religious groups do. E.g., Paul v. Watchtower Bible & Tract Soc'y of N.Y., Inc., 819 F.2d 875, 883 (9th Cir. 1987) ("The harms suffered by Paul as a result of her shunning by the Jehovah's Witnesses are clearly not of the type that would justify the imposition of tort liability for religious conduct. No physical assault or battery occurred.").

The Government also invited the jury to convict because Defendants "financially harmed victims by driving them into debt and not paying them for their labor." A-1222. More specifically, the Government stressed that Defendants accepted, and even encouraged, these "victims" to volunteer their services to their chosen religious organization. A‑908‑910; A‑1028‑1030; A‑1095-1103. But these "victims" were not coerced or defrauded into performing these volunteer services; they knew full well that their services would be unpaid, and they still chose to volunteer their efforts. A-947-48; A-1152-53; A872-76. This too is commonplace among religions: Under our constitutional tradition, it is a defining feature of religion that it relies on charitable contributions of money, goods, and services from its adherents. See generally James Madison et al., Remonstrance Against Religious Assessments (reproduced in full at Everson v. Bd. of Ed. of Ewing Twp., 330 U.S. 1, 63–72 (1947)). Indeed, many religions call for participants to tithe 10% of all their secular income. See Volokh, Addiction, 75 Emory L. J. at 1180 n. 5. But for First Amendment protections, a hostile jury could punish that practice as extortion because of religious pressure constituting "the threat of social ostracism or eternal damnation, or from the promise of community or of eternal." Id., at 1180.

The crux of the Government's charge was that the Defendants "forced" the purported victims to perform voluntary services through religious indoctrination and, more generally, made them feel reliant on OneTaste. See A-1236 (victims "felt like their whole world was OneTaste. It was their community, their friends, where they worked, and where they lived. And the defendants did all of this by design"). But such feelings of deliberately induced reliance on a religious community are entirely unremarkable in the religious context. See Volokh, Addiction, 75 Emory L. J. at 1183 (observing that a common technique among many religions is to "slowly lur[e] people into a community and a belief system that they may eventually find emotionally hard to leave, even if they feel some desire to leave").

Many Christians preach eternal damnation without Christ. Buddhists preach eternal suffering without dharma. Latter-day Saints encourage extensive participation in church callings, missionary service, and a tightly integrated congregational life. Countless religious traditions promise spiritual fulfillment, enlightenment, or eternal happiness through faithful adherence to their beliefs and practices. See Volokh, Addiction, 75 Emory L. J. at 1180, 1190. Many religions cause each of us to act and believe in ways non-adherents of our chosen path would find to be irrational or even "rank heresy." See United States v. Ballard, 322 U.S. 78, 86 (1944).

It is no answer for the Government to charge that these so-called victims felt "compelled" to perform the subject services because that compulsion was the product of religious conviction. If each of us are to be entrusted with the right to enter and exit our chosen religions at will, then each of us must also accept the risk that our chosen religions may cause us to donate time, money, or goods. The Court should find that the Free Exercise Clause prohibits this conviction.

[II.] The trial itself was not religiously "neutral."

Government's enforcement action, even under a facially religion-neutral generally applicable statute, violates the Free Exercise Clause when the enforcement of the statute is itself not "neutral," See Masterpiece Cakeshop v. Colorado C.R. Comm'n, 584 U.S. 617, 634 (2018). In Masterpiece Cakeshop, the government sought to enforce Colorado's public accommodations statute in part because of the religious motivations of a baker. Commissioners departed from neutrality by describing the baker's religious beliefs as "despicable" and characterized them as merely rhetorical. Id., at 635. Even "subtle departures from neutrality" on matters of religion are prohibited, not just when a legislative branch enacts a law but also when the executive branch enforces it. See id., at 638.

Just as in Masterpiece Cakeshop, the record in this case is replete with denigration of this particular religion. Ms. Gupta invited the jury to scrutinize OneTaste's vocabulary and the specific doctrines as evidence of wrongdoing. A-1232. She emphasized the specialized use of words or phrases "TurnON" (which seemed [synonymous] with the yoga phrase "state of flow"), "muggles" (meaning non-adherents of OneTaste), "matrix" (referring to "my fake reality of problems"), and "tumescence" (in the specialized spiritual sense of "bad energy that you were holding onto"), and the dichotomy between the "third dimension" (the "concrete world") and the "fourth dimension" ("the higher plane"), and asserted these words or phrases were being used to "indoctrinate the victims." A-1232, A-1235. This argument directly invited the jury to judge unfamiliar or strange religious concepts as proof of religious illegitimacy, which neither prosecutors nor jurors may do. See Masterpiece Cakeshop, 584 U.S. at 639; Fowler, 345 U.S. at 70.

Religions routinely use specialized phrasing like "saved," "possessed," "called," or "enlightened," which may appear unacceptable or incomprehensible to outsiders. That strangeness does not deprive OneTaste of First Amendment protections and certainly cannot underlie a felony criminal conviction, especially when the phrasing refers to spiritual or transcendental concepts. See Thomas v. Rev. Bd. of Indiana Emp. Sec. Div., 450 U.S. 707, 714 (1981). Quite the opposite: Our natural aversion to other religions is why we have tolerance protections enshrined in the First Amendment to begin with. See Ballard, 322 U.S. at 87; see also Marsh v. Chambers, 468 U.S. 783, 792 (1983).

The prosecutor also described OneTaste as a "sex cult." A-1223, A-1264. That label was inherently pejorative. See United States v. Helbrans, No. S219CR497NSR0102, 2021 WL 4778525, *17 (S.D.N.Y. Oct. 12, 2021) (prohibiting the Government from referring to defendants as being part of a "cult," prohibiting insinuations that "leaders brainwash or force members of the community to behave in or observe their religion in a certain way," and prohibiting "incendiary and irrelevant references" to the religious organization). The prosecutor was using this label as a rhetorical device to persuade jurors that OneTaste's teaching should be regarded with suspicion because they were unconventional. Just like in Masterpiece Cakeshop, this label was employed with the impermissible goal of suggesting the illegitimacy of a particular set of religious beliefs and practices. See 584 U.S. at 635.

The prosecutor argued, "that's not because OMing  was actually spiritual. They connected OMing to spirituality for legal protection, and so people would follow Nicole Daedone's teachings." A-1233; see also A-1381 ("They [Defendants] whittled them [victims] down by … indoctrinating them with so-called spiritual teachings and practices."). But what forms of meditation are "actually" spiritual and what are just "so-called" spiritual is not for secular courts to decide. It is no business of our secular government to "prescribe what shall be orthodox in … religion." Barnette, 319 U.S. at 642. The Government simply cannot put the legitimacy of religious or spiritual ideas on trial. Ballard, 322 U.S. at 86-88. Yet the Government did exactly that by arguing:

It is not okay to teach your employees that their spiritual purpose is to fuck the war out of men and that if they stray from the [path] set by OneTaste and by Nicole Daedone, they will be spiritually ruined.

And while there is a narrow zone in which a properly instructed jury can determine whether people's religious beliefs are sincerely held, United States v. Seeger, 380 U.S. 163, 165 (1965), no such instruction was given to the jury in this case. Quite the contrary, the District Court declined to provide jury instructions that any "alleged threats were covered by the First Amendment." A-1211. The District Court even warned defense counsel against referencing Defendants' First Amendment rights: "I'm not going to let you instruct the jury or even come close to instructing the jury on the First Amendment." A-1212. And the District Court refused to order a mistrial despite that the Government "ask[ed] the jury to hold their spiritual beliefs against them." A-1315-1316 (argument); A-1318 (denial).

The Government's rhetorical devices are a far cry from the neutrality required by Masterpiece Cakeshop. The Government was overtly hostile to Defendants' religion in itself and openly invited the jury to judge the legitimacy of OneTaste's religious doctrines and practices. It is no answer that the jury accepted the Government's invitation because the highest law of the land removes that power from legislator, judge, juror, and prosecutor alike. "If one could be sent to jail because a jury in a hostile environment found those teachings to be false, little indeed would be left of religious freedom." Ballard, 322 U.S. at 87.

[III.] Defendants were not charged with commercial sexual practices.

To be sure, nothing in this argument precludes the application of genuinely neutral laws to regulate commercial sexual behavior. For instance, an organization that sells members' or employees' sexual services for money can still be subject, under Employment Division v. Smith, to neutral and generally applicable bans on prostitution. Such laws can be applied without resorting to arguments about spiritual coercion, or claims that the defendant supposedly "indoctrinat[ed people] to believe that [she] was a guru and that her teachings were the path to enlightenment and spiritual growth." A-1222. It would not matter whether the  defendant "taught that orgasm was God." A-977. Commercial sale of certain services that lead to orgasm would be the crime, with no need to address the spiritual significance of the orgasm itself.

Likewise, if an employee claims that an employer required sexual services as a condition of employment, the employee could sue for quid pro quo sexual harassment, again a matter that is entirely religion-neutral. Indeed, the government could even criminalize such quid pro quo sexual harassment. See Tex. Penal Code Ann. § 39.03 (criminalizing sexual harassment under color of public office).

Unlike with the Government's expansive reading of the coerced labor statute, none of this would threaten religions that have a tradition of monasticism, or of religious labor as a calling. None of this would treat religious or spiritual teachings as "coercion." And none of this would treat such teachings as crimes when they lead people to feel moved, or even spiritually or religiously obligated, to perform certain tasks that are given to them by a spiritual or religious community.

Of course, in this case the Government chose not to prosecute under statutes banning commercial sale of sexual services—perhaps because there was no evidence that money was being exchanged in return for sexual activity. But these laws exist, and deal with genuine commercialization of sex. Likewise, laws banning rape and sexual assault exist, and deal with genuine physical coercion of sexual acts. There is no reason for a concern about possible commercialization of sex to be used to justify an overbroad reading of coerced labor statutes, which would apply far more broadly than just to sex.

Because the Government's theory of coercion rested in part on "indoctrination" into religious and spiritual beliefs and threats of excommunication from a religious and spiritual community, these criminal convictions cannot withstand Free Exercise Clause scrutiny….

#7752. 2026 Heating Oil Prices: Are They the Worst They’ve Ever Been, and Is There Any Way to Keep Costs From Skyrocketing?

Published Nov 2, 2026 2:27 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

If you are one of the 4 million households in the United States that rely on heating oil to power furnaces, boilers, and water heaters, you might be experiencing sticker shock when it comes to heating oil prices this season. The price has risen to about $6 per gallon compared to last year’s $3 per gallon.

According to the National Energy Assistance Directors Association, the cost to heat a home using heating oil is expected to rise by at least 50 percent across the region, including states like Maine, Massachusetts, and New York. In fact, Maine has been getting a lot of attention lately since the state relies heavily on this type of fuel, and prices have already reached 80 percent higher than just a year ago. Learn why heating oil is so expensive this year and what you can do to manage the “pain at the tank.”

Heating oil prices typically rise during the winter as demand increases heading into the heating season, says Lowell Richard, director of fuel operations at Townsend, a home service company based in New England that offers fuel delivery as well as HVAC and electrical services. “Over the past several months, global events and geopolitical uncertainty have driven significant increases in the cost of heating oil, propane, gasoline, diesel fuel, and other forms of energy,” he explains. With a shift in shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz due to the war with Iran, the cost of heating oil has gone up. The conflict between Russia and Ukraine has also impacted the global supply, leading to price hikes.

By comparison, propane prices are relatively unchanged from last year because propane has a different supply structure than heating oil. “Propane is a byproduct of both crude oil and natural gas processing, so its price is linked to both—natural gas prices tend to be steadier, while crude oil does fluctuate,” says Richard. “Additionally, propane has lower wholesale prices and adequate inventories. As a result, propane prices are typically steadier than heating oil prices.” It’s worth noting that propane prices vary by supplier and delivery volume, so Richard recommends checking with your local supplier for the current price.

If you are struggling to pay your heating bills, consider tapping into available resources in your area. “Every supplier is unique, but at Townsend, we offer several ways to help our customers spread out or control their costs,” explains Richard. “We have a variety of budget plans to help fit our customers’ financial needs. For example, automatic delivery is something we encourage because it typically offers better pricing and helps homeowners avoid emergency delivery fees.”

Fortunately, there are several ways for you to help offset high heating oil prices on your monthly bill. Try making one or more of the following changes in your home to keep heating costs manageable, and if suspect damage to your oil tank, have the tank checked and replaced if necessary.

Set your thermostat to a comfortable temperature, but keep in mind that setting it even a few degrees lower can save a noticeable amount on your energy costs, says Richard. “Intentionally setting your thermostat 7 to 10 degrees lower when you are sleeping or away can save up to 10 percent on annual heating costs,” Richard explains. Investing in a programmable or smart thermostat will help you set temperature preferences and schedules, even when you are not home.

Check all the doors, windows, and exterior walls for drafts, since your home can lose heat if ‌air is leaking out. “Replace old or missing weatherstripping around doors, windows, and pipe entry points, and seal cracks in your foundation if you have any,” suggests Richard.

Use a space heater so you can lower your thermostat a few degrees. Choose an energy-efficient model that has a thermostat, adjustable heat settings, sleep mode, and auto-off timers to avoid wasting energy. Always turn a space heater off when you leave the room.

Featuring three heating modes, quiet operation, and an attractive look, this efficient space heater earned “best overall” in our hands-on testing.

“Change your air filter every 30 to 90 days,” says Richard. “A clogged air filter will significantly impact how efficient your system is, so make this a regular habit.”

Maintain your heating system to ensure it is running as efficiently as possible, which in turn requires less energy to heat your home. “Get a fall tune-up to catch small problems before they become bigger, and therefore pricier, problems,” says Richard.

“If your water heater runs on heating oil, keep it set to 120 degrees Fahrenheit for safety and to save on energy costs,” notes Richard.

#7751. New Brennan Center Report on Curbing Executive Power

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Many of their recommendations are well-taken.

The NYU Brennan Center for Justice recently published a valuable report entitled "Seven Solutions to Rein In Abuses of Executive Power." The Brennan Center is well to the left of me. But I agree with the vast majority of their recommendations here. We do indeed have an overgrown executive, and it needs to be pared back. I particularly agree with the excellent section on constraining emergency powers:

With just a signature, presidents can declare a national emergency and unlock special powers contained in more than 130 statutory provisions. These run the gamut from the seemingly trivial to the near-dictatorial, including powers to shut down or take over communications infrastructure, freeze Americans' bank accounts, and control domestic transportation. They are intended for sudden, fast-moving crises that Congress can't address quickly or flexibly enough. But presidents of both parties have stretched the meaning of "emergency" far beyond reason, enabling them to draw from a growing stockpile of statutory authorities with few real safeguards.

There are currently 51 active states of emergency, and the longest-running has lasted 47 years.10 Any emergency that persists for generations is, by definition, not an emergency; it's a problem that can be addressed through ordinary lawmaking. Yet presidents have used emergency powers to bypass Congress and unilaterally advance their policy goals.11

The National Emergencies Act once allowed Congress to terminate emergencies with a simple majority vote and without the president's signature. But the Supreme Court struck down that procedure, known as a legislative veto, in 1983. Today, ending an emergency effectively requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers to override a presidential veto.

Congress should amend the National Emergencies Act to constrain executive overreach.12 Emergency declarations should expire automatically after 30 days unless Congress approves a one-year extension, renewable annually with Congress's assent. And presidents should be required to share detailed reports on their uses of emergency powers. Proposals along these lines have received widespread bipartisan support, with versions of these reforms overwhelmingly passing out of the relevant House and Senate committees in 2024.13

Additionally, Congress should amend specific emergency statutes whose extensive delegations of power and inadequate safeguards make them susceptible to misuse. Of particular concern is the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, the most frequently invoked presidential emergency authority.14 Sanctions imposed under this law can equate to a "financial death sentence" lasting years or decades.15 Although the Supreme Court blocked Trump's effort to use the law to set global tariffs, the potential for other abuses remains.

I completely agree, and have previously advocated similar reforms, myself. Brennan is right that IEEPA should be tightened up. While the Supreme Court did rule (in a case I helped litigate) that IEEPA cannot be used to impose tariffs, it still includes a lot of other dangerous powers.

I would add, as I did in this article, that invocations of emergency powers should be subject to  nondeferential judicial review, to ensure that they are used only in the event of genuine emergencies, not bogus ones. Congress would do well to amend relevant emergency statutes to make clear that such nondeferential judicial review is available.

I also strongly endorse Brennan's recommendations on constraining laws governing the domestic use of the military. The Supreme Court did strike down Trump's attempts to use bogus pretexts for federalizing the National Guard; the Ninth Circuit recently reinforced that ruling by rejecting the administration's broad definition of what qualifies as a "rebellion" justifying federalization. But, as the Brennan report indicates, there is still a lot of potential for abuse, especially when it comes to the Insurrection Act.

I also agree with the Brennan report's advocacy of constitutional amendments eliminating presidential immunity from criminal liability for acts undertaken in office, and barring him from pardoning crimes committed by "members of their inner circle, including immediate family members and senior administration officials" and those "convicted of crimes ordered by the president or committed on the president's behalf."

I doubt that these amendments have much chance of being enacted, given the extreme difficulty of passing any constitutional amendment. On the other hand, the reforms to emergency powers and domestic use of the military can be adopted through ordinary legislation. In some cases, they can also be bolstered by stronger judicial review under existing laws and provisions of the Constitution.

I do have a few disagreements with the report. For example, it is not clear to me that the Supreme Court's decision in Trump v. Slaughter goes as far as the authors suggest. The decision's scope remains uncertain. Among other things, it's not clear how wide a range of federal agencies it applies to and how to reconcile it with Trump v. Cook, decided on the same day. I also think they may overestimate Slaughter's impact, since most federal agencies are already not independent in the sense that there are legal constraints on the presidents' power to fire their heads.

I would also have liked to see more recognition that curbing excessive executive power requires curbing the scope of federal power generally. It is virtually impossible to have a federal government that regulates almost every aspect of human activity without simultaneously delegating vast - and often dangerous - discretion to the executive.

That said, the vast majority of the Brennan report's recommendations are well-taken. I hope future Democratic administrations and members of Congress act on them.

For those keeping score, it's worth noting that Brennan Center emergency powers expert Elizabeth Goitein, one of the authors of the report, is a long-time critic of abuses of emergency powers under Democratic administrations, as well as Republican ones. For example, she condemned President Biden's attempt to use emergency powers to effectuate massive student loan forgiveness. And so did I.

#7748. Court Blocks W. Va. AG's Subpoena to Environmentalist Nonprofits

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Part of the AG's argument was that the nonprofits relied on a climate change scenario, RCP8.5, that has been recently "retired."

From yesterday's decision by Judge Joseph Goodwin (S.D. W. Va.) in W. Va. Rivers Coalition, Inc. v. McCuskey:

The Attorney General of West Virginia has used the State's power to compel two citizen organizations to open ten years of their files: their drafts and internal arguments, the groups they have funded, the people who serve on their boards, the coalitions they have joined, and what they have told the agencies they petition. Neither organization markets goods nor services relevant to the subpoenas. The Attorney General identifies no consumer who was cheated, no sale, and no purchase made in reliance on anything either group said.

What these organizations do is argue in public about what coal, oil, and gas do to West Virginia's waters and climate. The State's chief legal officer, who has publicly condemned that advocacy, now demands to know how they reached their views and who stood with them.

The First Amendment forbids a State from using its investigative power that way, and I will not allow it while this case is pending.

The country was founded on the premise that a citizen owes the government no account of his opinions or of the people he holds them with. The Attorney General has demanded that two citizen organizations hand the State their working lives.

The State wants a decade of what they published, down to a note sent to a single person outside the organization, along with the unreleased drafts and the internal arguments over what to say. He demanded the names of the organizations that fund them and what each gave, and he has now withdrawn that demand. He still wants the groups they paid, the board members they share, the coalitions they joined, and the comments they filed with the agencies they were petitioning. Because the demand period runs to the date of compliance, the subpoenas reach new communications written while they remain outstanding. No demand identifies a consumer, a sale, or a statement anyone relied on. The subpoenas go into how these citizens arrived at their positions on public questions and who helped them get there.

The Plaintiffs in this case, West Virginia Rivers Coalition, Inc. ("WVRC") and 350.org, promote clean waters, reduced carbon emissions, and healthier lives for the people of West Virginia and beyond. They do not sell any service. They do not advertise a certain product of their own. Instead, they promote ideas. Some of that advocacy and some of those ideas are based, in part, on one model. For that, they have been subpoenaed and asked to turn over ten years' worth of information far beyond any use of that one model.

AG McCuskey's actions violate the protections afforded by the United States Constitution. The Plaintiffs, on this record, have only engaged in protected advocacy speech, not commercial speech. The subpoenas issued on the Plaintiffs trespass on their freedom of association, chill their exercise of the First Amendment, and deter others from engaging in similar conduct.

Because Plaintiffs are likely to succeed on the merits of their claim that the subpoenas violate their First Amendment freedom of association, and because the remaining injunction factors also favor Plaintiffs, their Motion for a Temporary Restraining Order, is GRANTED.

Attorney General McCuskey is enjoined from enforcing these investigative subpoenas for the next fourteen days as set out in the Conclusion of this Memorandum Opinion and Order….

Plaintiff WVRC is a river advocacy nonprofit corporation organized under the laws of West Virginia, and its "mission is to promote clean and healthy West Virginia waters for all." The nonprofit is committed to "clean water and healthy rivers through research, public education, policy advocacy, citizen water-quality monitoring, and engagement with state and federal agencies." It has a modest staff of 15 and an annual budget of approximately $2 million primarily funded by foundations and other organizations. WVRC regularly submits comments on proposed legislation, permits, and rules concerning water quality. And as this court is familiar, WVRC is a party litigant in multiple cases across the Fourth Circuit that challenge permits and approvals for infrastructure projects, pipeline projects, injection wells, and toxic discharges. Because of its litigation efforts, WVRC coordinates "with other organizations through shared counsel" about litigation strategy.

WVRC also engages in public education and information campaigns, including "statements about the effects of climate change in West Virginia's waters and communities, and about the environmental effects of fossil-fuel extraction, transport, and combustion." It is a member of multiple different coalitions committed to similar goals. To fund ts work, WVRC "solicits charitable contributions from the public through its website, mailings, emails, and events," but it does not publish the identities of its funders.

Plaintiff 350.org is a nonprofit corporation, and its "mission is to build a grassroots movement to end the use of fossil fuels and to accelerate the transition to renewable energy." The organization publishes information about climate change, organizes public demonstrations, and coordinates with other organizations with similar goals. 350.org also "solicits charitable contributions from the public through grant applications and through its website, mailings, emails, and events." Those grants and contributions are subject to opt-in confidentiality in some cases and agreed upon confidentiality in other cases.

And an excerpt from the court's First Amendment analysis (for more on RCP8.5, see this N.Y. Times article):

[T]he Court applies "exacting scrutiny" to compelled disclosures of protected First Amendment speech and association. To be a permissible intrusion on the First Amendment, "there must be 'a substantial relation between the disclosure requirement and a sufficiently important governmental interest.'" …

The subpoenas … "… concern[ ] an investigation into alleged unfair or deceptive acts or practices and other possible violations of the West Virginia Consumer Credit and Protection Act ('WVCCPA')." State code authorizes the Attorney General, if he "has probable cause," to "subpoena witnesses, compel their attendance, adduce evidence, and require the production of any matter which is relevant to the investigation."

Under West Virginia law, "[u]nfair methods of competition and unfair or deceptive acts or practices in the conduct of any trade or commerce are … unlawful." Trade or commerce "means the advertising, offering for sale, sale or distribution of any goods or services and shall include any trade or commerce, directly or indirectly, affecting the people of this state." "Unfair methods of competition and unfair or deceptive acts or practices" includes 16 different definitions including "[e]ngaging in any other conduct which similarly creates a likelihood of confusion or of misunderstanding."

Deploying these broad definitions, AG McCuskey's theory is that the Plaintiffs, environmental advocacy groups, published information, made comments, and advocated based on a study, the RCP8.5, that has been determined "implausible." According to AG McCuskey, this reliance, and subsequent advocacy, is a deceptive act or practice that affects the energy marketplace of West Virginia.

Begin with common sense—in what way could WVRC and 350.org violate the WVCCPA? They are not financial institutions, lenders, or creditors. They are not businesses seeking to make a profit by engaging with consumers. In fact, both are 501(c)(3) nonprofit organizations. They do not sell services of any kind. As explained, Plaintiffs are advocacy organizations committed to climate issues. Their missions are public education, dissemination of information, advocacy in support of their ideals, and public support of those who align with their beliefs. What little items they sell are merchandise bearing their names and logos. Surely these minimal sales from advocacy organizations are not the transactions the West Virginia legislature sought to protect consumers from….

Plaintiffs do not engage in commercial speech. By virtue of their missions as nonprofit environmental advocacy groups, their interests are not economic. Their interests include public education, funding environmental projects, modeling and projecting the effects of climate change, and contributing to a society that values clean air, clean water, and healthier lives. The fact that their advocacy touches on the economy is insufficient to be commercial speech. Therefore, Plaintiffs' protected speech and advocacy alleged in this case cannot be regulated under the WVCCPA.

Accordingly, I find that the WVCCPA cannot supply a "sufficiently important governmental interest" under the "exacting scrutiny" applied to freedom of association claims. I next turn to the severity of the "disclosure requirement" under the "exacting scrutiny" analysis….

As discussed, the subpoenas broadly assert that a violation of the WVCCPA might have occurred. And in his response, AG McCuskey admits that there may not be any WVCCPA violation. He does, however, have authority to issue subpoenas to investigate "whether a violation … has, in fact, occurred."

That violation, AG McCuskey argues, arises from only a few instances of Plaintiffs using a certain climate projection model, RCP8.5. Any publication born from that model, he asserts, is potentially unfair or deceptive. So to assess the breadth of the subpoenas and the compelled disclosure Plaintiffs are subjected to, the court turns to the subpoenas' demands. It is reasonable to assume that the demands would roughly track the RCP8.5-related violations and the allegations of unfair or deceptive trade practices.

Not so. The subpoenas ask for much more. The 16 categories of demands include every statement Plaintiffs have ever published about a West Virginia energy business with a "Climate Claim." But that demand is not limited to climate-related statements supported by the RCP8.5 model. It includes every climate-related statement that names a West Virginia energy business which is published and supported or informed, at least in part, by any model, study, project, plan, projection, or paper. Demand No. 4 is similarly broad: the subpoena demands every published projection concerning West Virginia and all documents related to those projections, without narrowing it down to those supported by the RCP8.5.

The rest of the demands do not even try to mask their broad and sweeping intentions. Donation requests, payments to third parties, and licensing and funding documents of all projects concerning West Virginia are demanded. Every document projecting costs and damages is demanded, as well as every report, study, model, or paper that the Plaintiffs directly or indirectly supported. Documents pertaining to internal considerations are demanded wholesale. So, too, are all documents pertaining to third-party communication and coordination in any fashion. And even with AG McCuskey's last-minute withdrawal of certain demands for donor information, Plaintiffs will still be obligated to disclose "board affiliation, coalition partners, grantees, agency submissions, internal deliberations and drafts, solicitation totals and targeting."

Plaintiffs call this a fishing expedition. In part, I agree. The subpoenas demand a large share of documents in Plaintiffs' control for the last ten years. But even on a fishing expedition, hoping to just get one bite in the vast and quiet water, a person brings a fishing pole. And in other cases, perhaps, a net. Here, AG McCuskey has abandoned both the fishing pole and the net. Instead, he has brought dynamite to the lake. Tossing a couple in, he hopes to catch something.

As stated, compelled disclosure that invades First Amendment protections can only stand if there is a substantial relation between what must be disclosed and a "sufficiently important governmental interest." Here, I find neither a sufficiently important government interest nor do I find a substantial relationship between the compelled disclosure and the government interest….

And the court also briefly notes plaintiffs' retaliation claim, without resolving it:

Plaintiffs have alleged substantial evidence to support their [retaliation] claim. AG McCuskey has publicly disparaged pro-environmental groups and has called for the DOJ to investigate similar groups. He has joined contentious litigation against environmental advocacy organizations. And the chasm between the subpoenas' demands and the purported basis for investigation suggests a retaliatory motive.

This phenomenon of state and federal investigation into the affairs of advocacy non-profits has begun to permeate our culture. The courts have enjoined civil investigative demands on comparable records. [Citations omitted. -EV]

However, because retaliation concerns the Attorney General's motive, I will reserve judgment on Count One until he can present evidence at a hearing for a preliminary injunction. Having already determined that an injunction is warranted on the basis of Count Two (freedom of association), the court declines to address the remaining counts….

Derek Teaney and Amanda Demmerle (Appalachian Mountain Advocates, Inc.) represent plaintiffs.

#7746. A Libertarian Perspective on the 2026 Election

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Why we should vote "Democrat by Default" for federal offices - with a few rare exceptions. I build on a post by political philosopher Dan Shapiro.

I was going to write a post about why, in this election, the right thing for libertarians to do is vote for Democrats for all federal offices, unless either 1) the Dem candidate is DSA, or 2) the GOP candidate is one of those very rare Republicans who oppose all or most of Trump's awful policies. But libertarian political philosopher Dan Shapiro beat me to it, in an excellent post at the Bleeding Heart Libertarian substack. I agree with the vast bulk of what he says. But I have a few additions and caveats that I will append after quoting a few key passages from Dan's post. Before getting into detail, I will note that I generally believe in voting for the lesser evil among those candidates with a realistic chance to win. Thus, unlike Dan, I don't usually vote for third party candidates, even in more normal times. If you're opposed to "lesser evil" voting on principle, we have a disagreement that goes  far beyond the present election. But I would urge you to check out my defense of that practice, where I explain why you should even vote for the evil Queen Cersei over the even more evil Sauron, if those are the only available choices.

I don't expect this post or Dan's will change the outcome of the election. They almost certainly won't. But they might still be helpful in thinking through big issues we face in the current political moment.

Most of my voting life I voted for the Libertarian Party when they advocated classical liberal/libertarian policies. Now those who care about and prioritize liberty and a free society—however they label themselves—should vote Democratic unless the candidate is a Democratic Socialist….

There's been so much criminality and misdeeds in the Trump administration that it's exhausting to cover it all, but keeping "the land of the free and the home of the brave" means remembering the essentials. I provide links when the points I make are not common knowledge and/or might be controversial.

January 6: Trump is the only presidential candidate in the US who refused to concede that he lost. He told a crowd to "fight like hell," and the mob then stormed the Capitol to try to overturn the results. The House impeached him for "incitement of insurrection," and 57 senators, including seven Republicans, voted to convict—short of the two-thirds required. After his campaign of lies and deception and pressuring election officials to falsify the results failed to overturn the election, he later pardoned all the perpetrators of the violence.

ICE: masked secret police who kidnap people and send them to hellholes in El Salvador, where they were subject to constant beatings, sexual abuse, and torture; to the Central African Republic, in the midst of a brutal civil war with severe human rights abuses; to Florida's "Alligator Alcatraz," where large numbers of detainees were held in cages the size of phone booths; and to Fort Bliss, Texas, where guards grabbed detainees' testicles while beating them. There've been zero consequences for this; indeed, Trump says they are "immune."

Not only were the deportations done without any notification to families or lawyers, but ICE has disappeared from databases those they seized so lawyers and families can't find them.

ICE and CBP have rammed people in their cars, dragged the occupants out, and rammed into houses without warrants. They have murdered, wounded, and assaulted protestors and ICE monitors—Alex Pretti and Renee Good, during the ICE occupation of Minneapolis, being the most publicized—but there have been many others.

There is now "expedited removal" for anyone undocumented, which means no hearing before a judge. (And this is even though immigration judges are—wrongly—a part of, and not independent of, the executive branch.) Indeed, Trump fired any immigration judge who disagreed with him or whom he perceived as not being deportation-friendly enough, and replaced the Board of Immigration Appeals, which has denied appeals for almost all deportation orders.

The administration removed TPS (temporary protected status) for immigrants fleeing violence and is deporting them to the very countries the State Department has declared unsafe—e.g., Haiti.

ICE apprehended immigrant parents after they dropped their kids off at school (see here, here, and here), as well as apprehending children and toddlers and using them as bait (the Liam Conejo Ramos incident)….

Trump sent Marines to LA, and National Guard troops to Chicago and DC. This violates a basic norm since the Founding and violates Posse Comitatus, a statute banning the military from policing.

Trump and FCC chairman Carr threatened talk shows and networks for dissenting political opinions.

As mentioned, ICE murdered, assaulted, and wounded protestors and ICE monitors.

The administration targeted people for their political views and for writing op-eds. Rochester resident David Streever sent a critical email to the director of ICE, and five months later, federal officers tracked his movements and staked out his New York City hotel as he returned from an overseas trip….

There is much more, including explanations of why the Democrats (with the notable exception of DSA types) are far less bad than this, despite their considerable flaws. I myself have written about the evils of the DSA here, explaining why they are comparable to MAGA nationalist Republicans.  In addition to the harm individual DSA members might cause if elected to office, it is important to reduce their numbers as much as possible, so as to minimize the chances that socialists could take over the Democratic Party, as MAGA nationalists have done with the GOP.

I have a few additions to Dan's arguments.

First, it is essential to consider the enormous scale of Trump's harmful and unjust immigration and trade policies. When it comes to setting issue priorities, scale matters a great deal. Even under normal administrations, immigration restrictions threaten the economic and civil liberties of American citizens (to say nothing of those of immigrants themselves) more than any other federal policy. Trump's vast expansion of exclusion and mass deportation has made things a lot worse. The liberty and well-being of millions of people are at stake.

Trump's trade policies seek to impose the highest tariff levels since those that gravely exacerbated the Great Depression, and also are a grave menace to the rule of law. Here too, we're talking about massive effects on the liberty and welfare of millions. Judicial review can and has helped curb these abuses (more on the tariff front than immigration). But there is much Congress can do to help, including curbing funding to ICE and other agencies complicit in wrongdoing. Congressional Democrats also plan to cut back executive tariff authority. That may not succeed while Trump remains in office, but can help set the stage for later progress.

Dan raises the issue of whether non-DSA Democrats might be worse than the Trump-era GOP on economic liberty issues. This becomes an easy issue if you recognize that immigration restrictions and tariffs are also violations of economic liberty. Due to their massive scale, Trump's actions in this area easily outweigh the very real economic policy flaws of non-DSA Dems. And then we have such things as his acquisition of federal government stakes in numerous private firms, something that even the most left-wing recent Democratic presidents didn't attempt. It's a dramatic example of how MAGA nationalists have dangerous economic policies similar to those of socialists.

It is also important to remember that a Democratic Senate could block Trump's horrible executive and judicial nominees. I don't want to see any more Pete Hegseths and RFK, Jrs. In Trump's first term, he had some good judicial nominees. In the second, he has mostly  bad ones (Emil Bove is a particularly egregious example). From a libertarian perspective, I'd rather have a standard liberal nominee fill the next Supreme Court vacancy (despite all the flaws such jurists have) than the type of right-winger Trump II is all too likely to nominate. Such a person would probably be selected for his willingness to turn a blind eye to executive abuses of power, trample civil liberties, and bulldoze constitutional obstacles to MAGA nationalist policies, such as federalism and separation of powers. There may well not be any Supreme Court vacancies, of course. But lower court nominations will arise, and they matter too.

Finally, I'm more hawkish than the average libertarian, and I think it's important to counter Trump's policies of undermining the Western alliance, and coddling mass-murdering dictators like Vladimir Putin and (to a lesser extent) Xi Jinping. We should care about defending liberty worldwide, not just in one country, especially since the two are interconnected. The Democrats (except for a few far-leftists) oppose this awfulness and could use control of Congress to help curb it.

In these and other areas, a Democratic-controlled Congress could not fully stop Trump's abuses. The executive has accumulated too much power for that, often in constitutionally dubious ways. But congressional control of nominations and purse strings can do much to constrain the executive at the margin. And electoral repudiation of Trump's abuses can reduce the risk that future presidents will imitate them.

I do have a few caveats to attach to Dan's otherwise compelling points:

First, Dan doesn't differentiate between elections for federal offices and those for state and local ones. I do. Beating the GOP in federal races is vital for countering Trump's awful agenda. At the state and local level, other issues are dominant, and Republicans are often better than Dems on the crucial issues of housing, state-level taxation, and state and local economic regulation. Which party is better on these and other state and local issues will vary from state to state. For example, red state Republicans are much better on the crucial issue of housing deregulation than blue state ones (who often back exclusionary zoning against Democratic reform efforts). Thus, it might make sense to vote for Republican candidates in some state and local races, but not others, depending on the issues involved.

Second, when it comes to the DSA problem, there can be difficult questions about what to do with Dem candidates who are not actual DSA members, but seem closely adjacent to them. Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is a notable example. He says he's not a socialist, but also is closely aligned with socialists like Bernie Sanders, and "influencer" Hasan Piker, the guy who - among other things - praises communist mass murderers like Mao Zedong.

In this post, I'm not going to try to adjudicate each individual candidate and race. I will merely say that if you're trying to figure out whether a non-DSA member is actually a socialist, two noteworthy indicators are 1) whether he or she supports government control of all or most of the economy and 2) whether they praise socialist despots abroad, such as Mao, Fidel Castro, and others. If the answers to one or both questions are "yes," that's a strong indication they might be socialists, and therefore not worth voting for, except perhaps against the very worst Republicans.

There is a similar calculation in identifying the few Republicans who have opposed Trump's worst policies. Here, key indicators are whether they have opposed his tariffs, his mass deportations, his kowtowing to Vladimir Putin, and his attacks on civil liberties. Sadly, Republican candidates with consistent strong records on all or most of these issues, are few and far between, though Republican criticism of the tariffs and policies towards Russia have picked up in recent weeks.

Finally, as Dan would agree, voting for Democratic candidates does not imply supporting everything the Democratic Party does, or abstaining from criticizing Democrats on the many occasions when they do bad things.

Elsewhere, I have argued that libertarians, in the current political moment, should seek an alliance with "abundance liberals." But alliance is not the same thing as total agreement. And the Democratic Party obviously includes various factions who are much worse than the abundance types. We should keep that in mind, even as we recognize that right now the Republicans are much worse.

#7745. Does Every Home Need a Bathtub? The Pros and Cons of Going Tub-Free

Updated Nov 2, 2026 2:35 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

There are shower people, and then there are bath people. While these two groups may be able to debate the advantages and disadvantages of having a bathtub in a home from sunrise to sunset, not every home needs a bathtub and some can’t do without.

Even though a bathtub may simply be nice to have, there may be other reasons to include or exclude a bathtub if you are thinking about future resale value and your investment. With luxury showers growing in popularity, homeowners’ needs for tubs are changing.

https://secure.money.com/embeds/embedder.js?v=1

Rachel Moussa, founder and Realtor at Blushwood Realty Group in Texas, says that when she first got into he unwritten rule was that there should be one bathtub on each floor that has a bedroom. For two-level homes with bedrooms upstairs and downstairs, there should at least one tub on each floor. We get that. If you love a good tub soak, you don’t want to have to schlep your bath salts, book, beverage, candle, and other gear to another floor.

This tub-per-floor rule, Moussa says, is no longer hard and fast. Whether you’re remodeling a bathroom or contemplating a home without a bathtub, here’s what to consider if you’re thinking about ditching the tub.

From a time and water waste perspective, showers have the upper hand. The average shower in the U.S. lasts approximately 8 minutes and uses approximately 16 gallons of water. A bath is a more languid affair. Sometimes soaks can last more than a half an hour and use around 70 gallons of water, which doesn’t include the water you might use to rinse off after a bath. The less water you use bathing, the more money you can save on your water bill.

The Keenray bucket towel warmer heats up in just 6 minutes and holds up to 2 bath towels measuring 70 x 40 inches. See our full review.

Shower people may not want a bathtub of any kind in their home, and might go as far as to remove a tub from their primary suite and put in a walk-in shower. If you plan to stay in the home long-term, nixing a tub really isn’t much to worry about. However, if you plan to put your house on the market in the near future and your floor plan doesn’t include a tub, understand that you’re automatically excluding some percentage of potential buyers.

After hundreds of sales and experience in renovating and flipping houses, Moussa says there are people who will not buy a house without a bathtub. In contrast, having a bathtub in a home is highly unlikely to tank a real estate transaction. So erring on the side of at least one tub in the house could make a difference in your ability to sell your home.

Moussa points out that jetted tubs can be pretty gross if they’re not taken care of properly. The interior pipes of jetted tubs that are not filtered or cleaned with appropriate chemicals can develop bacteria and microbial growth. When the jets turn on, this bacteria shoots into the tub along with the water, which can result in adverse health effects, including urinary tract infections and skin irritations or infections.

Families with young children or pets tend to rely heavily on tubs; many would consider a quality bathtub essential. Washing little ones in the kitchen sink may work while they are really small, but there comes a point when that doesn’t work anymore; tub baths, unlike showers, can get the kids clean while you stay dry. Similarly, a bathtub is often the easiest place to scrub dogs and other pets clean after they play outdoors.

RELATED: The Best Tub-to-Shower Conversion Kits to Update the Bathroom

Walk-in showers are generally better than tubs for seniors or those with mobility issues. Showers are easier to get into and out of than tubs are, and are thus usually preferred by those who are aging in place.

However, as Moussa mentions, houses do shift a little over time, so a curbless shower built at the right angle now may create an opportunity for water to pool years down the road. A shower that has even a small lip or curb can contain water better and eliminate future stress. Accessible walk-in tubs, which have with a side door to the bathtub for easy entry, are another option.

How often you plan to have a long, luxurious bath is another factor. If you don’t have a hot tub at your home, a hot bath is the next best thing. Creating a spa-like environment is a benefit many homeowners seek out when looking for a primary suite with a bathroom. A bathtub with a ledge around the top or near a source of natural light is another benefit that adds to the ambiance.

Many adults like baths because of the luxury associated with them, but Moussa points out that modern showers can be extravagant too. Large showers with frameless glass elevate the aesthetic of a bathroom. These showers often have multiple shower heads and settings, built-in seating, and plenty of space to shower without feeling cramped. The steam keeps you warm, and you get a constant water supply at your preferred temperature, unlike a tub where the water gets gradually cooler.

Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned and Loved About Them

From crown molding and built-ins to creaky floors and drafty windows, old houses are full of charm and challenges. So we’re celebrating all the things that make old homes worth loving, living in, and fixing up. Learn about historic house styles; find practical advice for maintaining your old home; and discover quirky, forgotten features you simply won’t find in new builds.

While you may be familiar with the convection space heaters used for decades, for more direct heat, infrared heaters are the better portable heating option. We discussed infrared technology with HVAC expert Justin Bohannon of Affordable Solutions HVAC & Electrical in Durham, North Carolina. He has a decade of experience working with heating systems and he agrees that these options are among the most energy-efficient and effective heaters on the market. As he attests, “infrared heaters directly heat objects and people in their path, rather than heating the entire room. This targeted heating approach can lead to energy savings as the heater focuses on heating the occupants instead of wasting energy on unused spaces.” To help shoppers decide on the best infrared heater for their needs, we put a variety of heaters through hands-on testing.

Choosing the best infrared space heater to supplement a primary heating system depends on the space it will heat, as well as budget, portability, safety features, and mounting. We rounded up a bunch of models for hands-on testing and can say, with confidence, that the following are among the best infrared heaters on the market. They range from electric wall heaters to rolling, floor-mounted options, plus plenty in between.

The addition of four durable caster wheels supports easy portability from room to room, and it includes a remote control that can operate the heater from across the room. What our tester says: “I can’t say enough about how nice it is to have a built-in humidifier to keep the air comfortable.”—Tom Scalisi, Product Reviews tester and writer

It features an adjustable thermostat for dialing in the ideal temperature and a large fan to spread the heat evenly throughout the space. One of the biggest drawbacks of forced-air-style heaters and space heaters is the impact they can have on air quality. Infrared heat is perfect for outdoor patios and decks, and the Briza infrared carbon heater makes a great choice. But, since it’s electric, it can also be used in a screened-in porch or a 3-season room, adding to its versatility.
